questions.title: Converging Batch POS and Streaming Clickstream in a Medallion Architecture
questions.prompt: You're designing a full medallion (bronze/silver/gold) architecture on Databricks for a retail analytics platform that ingests nightly batch POS exports (sales transactions, returns) and a continuous streaming clickstream feed (web/app browsing events) off the same storefront. Walk through what belongs at each layer and why, and be specific about where the batch and streaming sources actually converge into a single picture of the customer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Bronze stays raw and source-specific, and the two feeds get their own parallel bronze tables rather than being forced together early. The POS exports land via Auto Loader or a scheduled COPY INTO job as an append-only bronze_pos_transactions table, preserving the file's native grain and schema plus ingestion metadata (source file name, load timestamp). The clickstream lands via a Structured Streaming job reading from Event Hub/Kafka into bronze_clickstream_events, also append-only, also schema-preserved, with the stream's offset/watermark tracked through checkpointing. Nothing is deduplicated, cleaned, or joined yet -- bronze's only job is to be a faithful, replayable copy of what arrived, because the grain of a sales transaction and the grain of a page-view event are fundamentally different things and forcing them into one shape this early loses information you can't get back.

Silver is where each source gets cleaned and conformed independently, but still kept separate. Silver POS resolves returns/voids against their original transactions, standardizes currency/timezone, and enforces quality constraints (no null transaction IDs, valid store IDs). Silver clickstream deduplicates retried events, filters bot traffic, and sessionizes raw page-views into sessions using a watermark-based groupBy on session gaps. Both are still at their own grain -- transaction grain and session/event grain -- because merging them here would mean picking one grain and throwing away the other's detail.

The real convergence point is gold, where both are conformed against shared dimensions (customer, product, date, store) into an analytics-ready model -- a customer_360 or product_performance gold table that joins purchase facts from silver POS with browsing-behavior facts from silver clickstream via the shared customer or session-to-purchase linkage. That's the layer built for cross-source analysis, so it's the right place to pay the join cost once rather than scattering ad-hoc joins across every downstream query. The one exception worth naming: if there's a genuine near-real-time requirement -- say, personalizing the site based on a customer's browsing behavior from the last five minutes plus their purchase history -- that specific need justifies an earlier, narrower stream-static join in silver (enriching the live clickstream against a static snapshot of customer/purchase data) rather than waiting for a batch gold refresh, but that's a deliberate exception for a specific use case, not the general convergence strategy.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the team to resist the urge to join these two sources early just because they both describe the same customer. Bronze is two separate tables, full stop -- bronze_pos_transactions from the nightly batch drop, bronze_clickstream_events from the streaming job -- each one just a faithful raw copy of what came in, no cleaning, no joining, because they're different grains and trying to force them together before you've even cleaned either one just creates a mess you have to undo later.

Silver is still two tables, but now each one is actually usable on its own -- POS silver has returns resolved and quality rules enforced, clickstream silver is deduped and sessionized. They stay separate at this layer because a transaction and a session are genuinely different things, and collapsing them too early throws away detail you'll want downstream.

Where they actually come together is gold, through shared dimensions like customer and date -- that's where you build the customer_360 or product performance view that actually answers cross-source questions, and it's the one place I'd want to pay that join cost, not fifty different places. The one thing I'd flag as an exception: if there's a real need for near-real-time personalization using live browsing behavior, that's worth a targeted stream-static join in silver just for that use case -- but that's a carve-out for a specific requirement, not how I'd design the general pipeline.
commonMistakes: Joining raw bronze streaming and batch data directly, before either side has been cleaned or deduplicated
Treating medallion as one table per layer instead of parallel per-source bronze/silver tables that converge downstream
Collapsing transaction grain and event grain together too early and losing information neither side can recover
Forgetting to handle late-arriving batch data relative to clickstream silver that's already processed and sessionized
Defaulting every near-real-time requirement into gold instead of recognizing when a targeted earlier stream-static join is justified
keyPoints: Bronze is raw and source-specific -- one table per source, no joining
Silver cleans and conforms each source independently while preserving its own grain
Gold is the real convergence point, joined through shared dimensions
A genuine near-real-time use case can justify an earlier, narrow stream-static join in silver
Medallion is parallel pipelines merging downstream, not a single linear chain

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct bronze design per source (raw, separate, append-only)
Correct silver design per source including cleaning/dedup at the right grain
Correctly identifies gold as the convergence point with sound reasoning
Addresses the near-real-time exception and when an earlier join is justified
Clarity and structure

questions.title: Unity Catalog Governance Across Dev, Test, and Prod Without Manual Re-Granting
questions.prompt: You're designing a Unity Catalog governance structure for a data platform with multiple teams and separate dev, test, and prod Databricks workspaces. Walk through how catalogs, schemas, and access grants should be organized so that promoting a new table or schema from dev to prod doesn't require someone to manually re-grant every permission by hand.
questions.modelAnswer:
Start with the structure: one catalog per environment (dev, test, prod) sitting inside the same metastore, each bound to only its own workspace via workspace-catalog bindings -- this is the piece that actually enforces the boundary, since without it a grant on the prod catalog could still be reachable from the dev workspace. Inside each environment's catalog, schemas are organized by team or domain (finance, marketing, operations), mirrored identically across all three catalogs so dev.finance, test.finance, and prod.finance have the same shape.

Grants are made to Entra ID groups synced into Databricks, never to individual users -- a finance_analysts group gets SELECT on the finance schema in whichever catalog is relevant to them, and because Unity Catalog's privilege model is hierarchical, a grant at the catalog or schema level applies to everything created underneath it unless explicitly revoked, so a new table added to prod.finance tomorrow inherits today's grants automatically without anyone touching permissions again.

The piece that actually solves the 'don't re-grant manually on promotion' problem is treating the grants themselves as code. The same Terraform module that provisions dev.finance's schema and grants is applied against test.finance and prod.finance with only the catalog name and group mappings changed as variables -- so when a new schema or table gets promoted, the IaC pipeline applies the identical, already-proven grant pattern to prod instead of a person reconstructing it by hand in the UI, which is both slower and where real environments actually drift from each other. Storage credentials and external locations should also be scoped per environment so a dev service principal can never read prod's underlying storage, independent of whatever Unity Catalog grants say.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd set this up: one catalog per environment, each one locked to its own workspace through a workspace-catalog binding, because that's the actual enforcement boundary -- grants alone don't stop a dev user from reaching prod if the catalog isn't bound away from the dev workspace. Inside each catalog, schemas are laid out by team, same shape in dev, test, and prod.

All the grants go to Entra groups, never individual people, and because Unity Catalog grants cascade down from catalog to schema to table, a new table showing up in prod next month already has the right permissions the moment it's created -- nobody has to remember to grant it.

The actual fix for 'don't re-grant by hand on promotion' is that the grants live in Terraform, not in someone's memory of what they clicked in dev. The same module stands up dev.finance and prod.finance, just with different variables, so promoting a schema means running the pipeline against a new catalog, not reconstructing permissions in the UI -- which is exactly where environments quietly drift apart from each other. And I'd scope the storage credentials per environment too, so even a mistake in Unity Catalog grants can't let a dev principal touch prod's actual data.
commonMistakes: Granting permissions to individual users instead of Entra ID groups
Sharing one catalog across all environments with no workspace-catalog binding, letting dev reach prod data
Manually re-clicking grants in the UI for every new table in prod instead of applying them as code
Not relying on Unity Catalog's hierarchical/inherited grants, so every new object needs its own manual grant
Leaving storage credentials and external locations shared across environments instead of scoped per environment
keyPoints: Catalog per environment, each bound only to its own workspace
Schemas organized by team/domain, mirrored identically across environments
Grants go to Entra ID groups, never individuals
Inherited/hierarchical grants mean new objects don't need re-granting
Grants-as-code (Terraform) applied identically across environments is what removes manual re-granting
Storage credentials/external locations scoped per environment independent of catalog grants

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct catalog-per-environment and workspace-catalog binding design
Group-based least-privilege grant design
Identifies grants-as-code/Terraform as the actual fix for manual re-granting on promotion

Clarity

questions.title: Lambda or Kappa for a Platform Needing Both Real-Time and Reprocessable History
questions.prompt: A new streaming analytics platform needs to serve real-time dashboards and also support reprocessing the same historical event data when the business logic changes. Decide between a Lambda architecture and a Kappa architecture for this platform, and justify it with the real operational tradeoffs -- code duplication, reprocessing cost, and consistency between views.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lambda architecture runs two separate layers against the same raw data: a batch layer that reprocesses full history for accuracy, and a speed layer that produces fast, approximate real-time results, with a serving layer merging the two views for consumers. The real cost of Lambda isn't the extra infrastructure -- it's that the batch and speed layers almost always end up implementing similar transformation logic in two different codebases (a Spark batch job and a separate streaming job), and those two implementations drift apart over time as each gets patched independently, which is exactly the kind of inconsistency that erodes trust in the numbers once someone notices the real-time dashboard and the nightly batch report don't agree.

Kappa architecture collapses this into a single stream-processing pipeline: there's no separate batch layer, because 'reprocessing' just means replaying the event log from an earlier offset through the same streaming job, using the same code, to produce a new, corrected view. That only works if the underlying log (Kafka, Event Hubs with tiered/long-term retention) actually retains enough history to replay from, and if the stream processing engine (Structured Streaming, Flink) can sustain the throughput needed to replay a large volume of historical events in a reasonable window -- which modern stream processors genuinely can, but it's not free; replaying months of history through a streaming engine is still a real compute cost, just paid through the same pipeline rather than a second one.

For this specific requirement -- real-time dashboards plus reprocessable history from the same event data -- I'd recommend Kappa, because the dominant risk here is exactly the one Kappa eliminates: two codebases quietly producing different answers to the same question. The requirement for safe replay does mean the streaming transforms need to be idempotent and deterministic (same input events always produce the same output, regardless of how many times they're replayed), which is a real design constraint, but it's a more honest cost than maintaining parallel logic. I'd only fall back to Lambda if the reprocessing logic needed to diverge meaningfully from the real-time logic -- for example, a batch-only algorithm or a heavy join that genuinely isn't practical to express in the streaming engine -- in which case accepting the dual-codebase risk is the lesser evil.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd frame the choice around one question: do we want to maintain two codebases that are supposed to agree with each other, or one codebase we replay? Lambda is the two-codebase answer -- a batch job for accurate historical reprocessing and a separate streaming job for fast real-time results, merged at serving time. The problem isn't that it's more infrastructure, it's that those two jobs drift apart in practice, and then someone notices the dashboard and the nightly report don't match.

Kappa is the one-codebase answer -- reprocessing just means replaying the Kafka log from an earlier offset through the same streaming job that handles real-time traffic. That requires the log to actually retain enough history to replay, and replaying a lot of it isn't instant, but it's the same cost paid through one pipeline instead of two slightly-different ones.

Given this platform needs both real-time views and reprocessable history off the same data, I'd go with Kappa -- the main risk I'd be worried about otherwise is exactly the inconsistency problem Kappa avoids. The real design cost is making sure the streaming transforms are idempotent and deterministic so a replay actually produces a consistent result. I'd only switch back to Lambda if the reprocessing logic needed something fundamentally different from what the streaming engine can reasonably do -- a heavy batch-only algorithm, say -- in which case I'd accept the dual-codebase risk because there's no honest way around it.
commonMistakes: Assuming Kappa eliminates batch-scale processing entirely rather than unifying it via replay through the same engine
Not accounting for log retention sizing/cost needed to make Kappa's replay-based reprocessing actually work
Defaulting to Lambda out of familiarity without acknowledging the logic-drift/consistency risk it carries
Not addressing the idempotency/determinism requirement that safe replay in Kappa depends on
Ignoring the real compute cost of replaying large historical volumes through a streaming engine versus a dedicated batch engine
keyPoints: Lambda separates batch and speed layers, risking logic drift and inconsistent results between them
Kappa unifies everything into one replayable stream-processing pipeline
Kappa reprocessing means replaying the log through the same code, which requires sufficient retention
Kappa depends on idempotent, deterministic transforms for safe, consistent replay
Choose Kappa for codebase consistency when feasible; fall back to Lambda only when reprocessing truly needs different logic

Correctly explains Kappa architecture and its replay mechanics
Addresses log retention and replay cost practicalities
Gives a justified recommendation with sound reasoning

questions.title: Kafka Partitioning for a Multi-Tenant SaaS Platform With Wildly Uneven Tenants
questions.prompt: You're designing the Kafka topic and partition strategy for a high-throughput, multi-tenant SaaS platform where each tenant's event volume varies by orders of magnitude -- a handful of enterprise tenants dwarf hundreds of small ones. Walk through your partitioning key choice, how you'd avoid a big tenant creating a noisy-neighbor hot partition, and the retention tradeoffs.
questions.modelAnswer:
The naive choice -- keying every message by tenant_id -- guarantees that every event from a given tenant lands in exactly one partition, which preserves per-tenant ordering but also means a single partition's throughput ceiling becomes that tenant's throughput ceiling. For the handful of enterprise tenants producing orders of magnitude more volume than everyone else, that single partition becomes a hot, overloaded partition no matter how many partitions the topic has overall, because partition count doesn't help a key that always hashes to the same place.

The fix is a composite or tiered key strategy. For most tenants, a composite key -- tenant_id plus a finer-grained sub-key like user_id, device_id, or entity_id -- spreads a given tenant's events across several partitions while still preserving ordering within that finer-grained key, which is usually the ordering guarantee that actually matters (events for the same user/device stay in order, even if events for the same tenant across different users don't need a strict total order). For the small number of genuinely oversized 'whale' tenants, I'd go further and isolate them onto dedicated topics (or a dedicated partition range) entirely, so their volume physically can't create contention for the shared multi-tenant topic the smaller tenants use -- a tiered strategy where tenant size, not just tenant identity, decides the topic/partition assignment.

One real constraint to design around up front: partition count can be increased later but never decreased, and increasing it reshuffles the key-to-partition mapping for every existing key, breaking the very ordering guarantee you were relying on -- so partition count needs to be sized with reasonable headroom for growth from day one, not fixed small and 'grown into.' For retention, I'd keep Kafka's own retention short and tiered -- just enough to support real-time processing and a reasonable reprocessing window -- and sink the data into Delta Lake, partitioned by tenant and date, for genuine long-term storage and historical analysis, rather than trying to make Kafka itself the system of record for months of history. That also helps with tenant-level compliance needs like data deletion, which are much easier to honor against partitioned storage in a lakehouse than against a long-retention Kafka log.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd flag the obvious trap first: if you key purely by tenant_id, your biggest tenants each get pinned to one partition, and that partition's throughput ceiling becomes that tenant's throughput ceiling, no matter how many partitions the topic has. That's the noisy-neighbor problem right there, baked into the key choice.

For most tenants, I'd use a composite key -- tenant plus something finer like user or device -- so a given tenant's traffic spreads across multiple partitions while still keeping the ordering that actually matters, which is usually per-user or per-device, not a strict total order across the whole tenant. For the handful of genuinely huge tenants, I'd isolate them onto their own topic entirely rather than trying to tune around them in the shared topic -- their scale is a different problem than the long tail of small tenants.

One thing I'd make sure the team knows up front: you can add partitions later, but you can't remove them, and adding them reshuffles where existing keys land, which breaks ordering guarantees you were counting on. So I'd rather size partition count with real headroom from day one than try to grow into it. And for retention, I wouldn't lean on Kafka to hold months of history -- short retention in Kafka, sink everything into Delta Lake partitioned by tenant and date for the long-term story, which also makes tenant-level deletion requests for compliance a lot easier to actually honor.
commonMistakes: Keying purely by tenant_id, so a single large tenant's events are pinned to one hot partition
Assuming adding more partitions later preserves existing keys' partition assignment (it doesn't; rehashing breaks ordering)
Not isolating oversized 'whale' tenants onto their own topic or dedicated partition range
Applying one uniform retention policy regardless of tenant-level compliance/deletion requirements
Scaling partition count arbitrarily high without weighing the rebalance and broker overhead cost
keyPoints: Pure tenant_id keying creates hot partitions for large tenants regardless of total partition count
A composite/finer-grained key or dedicated topics for whale tenants isolates noisy neighbors
Partition count changes are one-way and reshuffle key-to-partition mapping, so plan ahead
Balance partition count against per-partition throughput needs and rebalance/broker overhead
Keep Kafka retention short and sink to Delta Lake, partitioned by tenant and date, for long-term storage
Tenant-level compliance/deletion needs are easier to honor in partitioned lakehouse storage than in Kafka's own log

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the noisy-tenant hot partition problem and its root cause
Proposes a sound composite-key/tiered partitioning strategy
Addresses partition count growth and rebalancing tradeoffs
Addresses retention tradeoffs including compliance needs

questions.title: Where Exactly-Once Really Comes From in a Kafka-to-Delta Pipeline
questions.prompt: Design an ingestion path that gets data from Kafka into a Delta Lake table with end-to-end exactly-once semantics. Walk through where the real guarantee actually comes from -- idempotent writes, checkpointing -- versus where 'exactly-once' is really just 'effectively-once' achieved through idempotent design.
questions.modelAnswer:
The mechanism that actually prevents reprocessing already-committed data is the coordination between Structured Streaming's checkpointing and Delta's atomic transaction commit. Each micro-batch's Kafka offsets are recorded in the checkpoint location, and the corresponding write to the Delta table is committed as an atomic transaction in Delta's log; Structured Streaming's Delta sink coordinates these two things so that on a failure and restart, Spark resumes from the last successfully committed offset and does not reprocess a micro-batch that already landed in the table. That's the real, documented guarantee for Structured Streaming writing to Delta -- it's correctly described as exactly-once processing semantics for that specific hop.

What it does not give you is protection against duplicate events that existed before they ever reached that hop. Kafka's idempotent producer and transactional APIs prevent a producer's own retries from creating duplicate messages inside Kafka itself, but they say nothing about whether the upstream system generating those events already sent the same logical event twice for its own reasons (a retried API call, a replayed message from yet another upstream system). That's why engineers who've actually run this in production call it 'effectively-once' rather than true exactly-once: the guarantee you get from checkpointing plus atomic commits is real, but the guarantee you need at the business level requires an additional layer of idempotent design on top of it.

That additional layer is a business-level dedup key -- an event_id or equivalent uniqueness attribute carried in the payload -- enforced through a MERGE into the Delta table (matching on that key, inserting only when it's not already present) rather than a plain append. Combined with checkpointing to avoid reprocessing committed micro-batches, and MERGE on a business key to guard against duplicate events that arrive more than once across different micro-batches or even different job runs, you get a system that behaves like exactly-once in practice -- which is the honest way to describe it, rather than pointing at any single Kafka or Spark setting and calling it solved.
questions.professionalAnswer:
If someone asks me where exactly-once 'comes from' here, I'd point to two different things and be clear they're solving two different problems. The first is Structured Streaming's checkpoint plus Delta's atomic commit -- that combination means if a micro-batch already landed in the Delta table and then the job crashes and restarts, Spark picks up from the last committed offset instead of reprocessing what already succeeded. That part is a real, solid guarantee for that specific hop.

What that doesn't cover is a duplicate event that was already duplicated before it got to Kafka -- Kafka's idempotent producer only stops the producer's own retries from creating extra copies inside Kafka, it has nothing to say about whether the source system sent the same logical event twice in the first place.

So the piece that actually closes that gap is doing a MERGE into the Delta table keyed on a business-level event ID, instead of a plain append -- that way, even if the same event shows up twice across different micro-batches, it only lands once in the table. Checkpointing stops you from reprocessing what already succeeded, and the MERGE on a dedup key stops a duplicate event from landing twice even if it does show up again. Together those two behave like exactly-once in practice, which is really why people call it 'effectively-once' instead of pretending any single setting solves the whole problem.
questions.example:
# Structured Streaming -> Delta with checkpointing + idempotent MERGE
df.writeStream \
  .format("delta") \
  .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders") \
  .foreachBatch(lambda batch_df, batch_id: (
      DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.orders")
        .alias("t")
        .merge(batch_df.alias("s"), "t.event_id = s.event_id")
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute()
  )) \
  .start()
commonMistakes: Believing Kafka's exactly-once producer configuration alone solves end-to-end deduplication
Mishandling checkpointing -- e.g. deleting the checkpoint directory on redeploy, causing reprocessing or data loss
Using plain append writes instead of MERGE, so a replayed micro-batch inserts duplicate rows
Skipping a business-level dedup key, so application-level exactly-once is never actually achieved
Treating 'exactly-once' as a single setting rather than a combination of checkpointing, atomic commits, and idempotent writes
keyPoints: True end-to-end exactly-once is achieved through idempotent design, not a single mechanism
Structured Streaming checkpointing plus Delta's atomic commit prevents reprocessing already-committed micro-batches
Kafka's idempotent/transactional producer only dedups within Kafka, not duplicates from the original source
MERGE on a business-level dedup key provides true row-level idempotency across micro-batches
Preserving the checkpoint location across restarts and redeploys is critical

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains checkpointing plus atomic Delta commit mechanism
Correctly distinguishes Kafka-level from application-level duplicate prevention
Proposes the correct idempotent write pattern (MERGE on a dedup key)
Accurately frames this as 'effectively-once' rather than a single guarantee

questions.title: A Combined CI/CD Pipeline for Databricks Code and Terraform Infrastructure
questions.prompt: Design a combined CI/CD pipeline that deploys both Databricks notebook/pipeline changes and the underlying Terraform-managed infrastructure for a data platform together. Walk through ordering -- infra before code or the other way around -- environment promotion, and rollback for each layer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Infra generally has to be in place before the code that depends on it runs -- a job can't use a Unity Catalog schema, a cluster policy, or a secret scope that Terraform hasn't provisioned yet. But that doesn't mean they belong in one lockstep pipeline; it means infra deploys through its own pipeline, on its own cadence (infra changes far less often than notebooks/jobs do), with its own gating -- plan review, policy checks via something like Checkov or tflint, and a required approval for anything touching prod. The code pipeline, packaging notebooks/jobs/pipelines as versioned Databricks Asset Bundles, runs separately and more frequently, and only needs to wait on the infra pipeline when a specific code change actually depends on an infra change that hasn't landed yet.

Both pipelines promote through the same dev -> test/staging -> prod sequence, each with environment-specific configuration -- infra via tfvars per environment, code via DAB's own per-environment target configuration -- and each gated by automated validation appropriate to that layer: infra gets plan review and policy-as-code checks before apply, code gets unit and integration tests run against the dev or staging workspace before promotion. Prod promotion for both layers requires an explicit manual approval, but they're still two separate approvals for two separate changes, not one combined gate that forces every code deploy to also re-approve infra.

Rollback also has to stay decoupled, because conflating the two makes a simple code bug into an infra incident. A bad notebook or job change rolls back by redeploying the previous version of the Databricks Asset Bundle -- since it's a versioned, git-tagged artifact, that's a fast, low-risk redeploy that doesn't touch infrastructure at all. A bad infra change rolls back by reverting to a previous Terraform state/module version and re-applying -- never by manually editing resources in the portal, which breaks the state's accuracy going forward. Keeping these two rollback paths independent is exactly why the pipelines shouldn't be merged into one: the far more common failure mode is a code bug, and you want that fixable in minutes without touching infra at all.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My rule of thumb: infra needs to exist before the code that depends on it runs, but that's a dependency, not a reason to merge the pipelines. Infra gets its own pipeline that runs less often, with stricter gating -- plan review, policy checks, a real approval for prod -- because infra mistakes are expensive and slow to notice. Code -- notebooks, jobs, pipelines packaged as Databricks Asset Bundles -- gets its own pipeline that runs more often, with its own tests, and it only waits on the infra pipeline when a specific change genuinely needs something infra hasn't provisioned yet.

Both go through the same dev -> staging -> prod promotion sequence, each with their own environment-specific config and their own tests appropriate to what they are, and prod for either one needs an actual approval -- but two separate approvals, not one that drags code changes into re-approving infra every time.

Where I'd really push to keep them separate is rollback. If a notebook breaks something, I want to redeploy the previous version of that bundle in minutes and be done -- no infra involved. If an infra change breaks something, that's a Terraform state revert and a careful re-apply, never a manual portal edit that leaves the state lying about reality. Code bugs are the far more common failure, and the whole point of keeping these pipelines decoupled is that fixing one doesn't require touching the other.
commonMistakes: Coupling infra and code into one monolithic pipeline so every code change risks triggering unnecessary infra changes
Giving infra changes the same light-touch approval as routine code deploys instead of stricter gating
Manually applying Terraform for prod instead of running it through a gated pipeline
Having no versioned rollback story for jobs/notebooks, relying on manual redeploy from memory
Not testing infra changes (plan review, policy-as-code) with the same rigor code changes get before promotion
keyPoints: Infra generally deploys ahead of dependent code, but as a separate, less frequent, more strictly gated pipeline
Both layers promote through the same dev -> test -> prod sequence with their own environment-specific configuration
Databricks Asset Bundles version and parameterize code deployments analogous to how Terraform modules version infra
Rollback means redeploying a prior versioned artifact or state, never manual edits
Decoupled pipelines mean a code rollback never requires touching infra, and vice versa

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ordering/dependency reasoning between infra and code pipelines
Correct promotion and environment-gating design for both layers
Mentions Databricks Asset Bundles or an equivalent versioned code deployment mechanism
Correct, decoupled rollback strategy for infra versus code

questions.title: Sharding a Ride-Sharing Platform's Real-Time Analytics at Hundreds of Thousands of Events a Minute
questions.prompt: Design the data architecture -- ingestion, partitioning/sharding, and serving layer -- for a ride-sharing company's real-time analytics platform at a scale of hundreds of thousands of trip events per minute. Walk through how you'd shard or partition the data and what tradeoffs that creates for queries that need to span multiple shards.
questions.modelAnswer:
For ingestion at this volume, events (location pings, trip state changes) flow through Kafka or Event Hubs partitioned by a key that actually matches the platform's query locality -- geographic region or driver ID, not trip_id, since trip_id has no locality benefit and would just scatter related events randomly. Partitioning by geo-cell or city keeps a given region's event sequence ordered within its partition, which matters for dispatch-adjacent processing, and lets partition count and consumer parallelism scale against real throughput needs rather than an arbitrary default.

For sharding/storage, geography is the natural sharding key for the same reason: the overwhelming majority of ride-sharing queries -- supply/demand matching, surge pricing, dispatch -- are geo-local, so sharding by city or region means most queries stay within one shard and each shard's compute and storage scale independently. The real tradeoff shows up for queries that cross shard boundaries -- a platform-wide 'total trips this hour across every city' query, or a trip that spans two regions -- which require a fan-out/scatter-gather across shards and a merge step, adding real latency and complexity that a single-shard query never pays. The mitigation is maintaining a separate, incrementally updated global rollup -- each shard's gold-layer city aggregates feeding a platform-wide summary table -- so cross-shard analytical queries hit a small pre-aggregated dataset instead of live scatter-gather across every operational shard. Skew is also a real concern here: a mega-city shard (New York, Tokyo) can dwarf a small-city shard, so I'd sub-partition within large shards (by geo-cell or H3 hex) to avoid one city becoming a bottleneck on its own, the same underlying problem as a noisy tenant in a multi-tenant system.

For the serving layer, I'd deliberately separate two different needs rather than forcing one store to do both: a low-latency 'current state' store (nearest-driver matching, live location) optimized for point lookups and recent data, and a separate analytical serving store (Delta Lake, partitioned by date and region, Z-ordered on commonly filtered columns like city_id) optimized for aggregation over time. Trying to serve both dispatch-grade operational latency and historical analytical aggregation from the same store forces compromises neither workload should have to make, and the cross-shard rollups used for dashboards can tolerate seconds-level eventual consistency, which the live dispatch path cannot -- a reasonable tradeoff to accept for query speed on the analytics side.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd key ingestion by something with real locality -- geo-region or driver, not trip_id, since trip_id scatters related events with no benefit. That keeps a region's event sequence ordered within its Kafka partition, which matters for anything downstream that cares about sequence.

For sharding, geography is the obvious key here because almost every query this platform runs -- matching supply and demand, surge pricing, dispatch -- is local to one city or region anyway, so most queries never leave their shard. The tradeoff I'd flag up front is the query that does cross shards -- a platform-wide total, or a trip spanning two regions -- that's a scatter-gather across shards, and it's slower and more complex than a normal query by nature. I'd handle that by keeping a separately maintained global rollup that each shard feeds incrementally, so the cross-shard dashboard query hits a small pre-aggregated table instead of fanning out live across every shard every time. I'd also expect a few mega-city shards to dwarf the small ones, so I'd sub-partition those by geo-cell to avoid one city becoming the bottleneck for the whole shard.

For serving, I wouldn't try to make one store do both jobs. Dispatch and nearest-driver matching need a low-latency operational store built for point lookups; the analytics dashboards need a Delta Lake-style store built for scanning and aggregating over time. I'd let the cross-shard analytical rollups be eventually consistent, seconds of staleness, because that's a fine tradeoff for query speed on the dashboard side -- it's just not a tradeoff I'd accept on the live dispatch path.
commonMistakes: Sharding or partitioning by trip_id, which has no locality benefit and scatters related events randomly
Not planning for cross-shard rollups, discovering at query time that global aggregates require slow live scatter-gather over every shard
Ignoring severe geographic skew (mega-cities) and ending up with one oversized, bottlenecked shard
Conflating the real-time dispatch/matching system's latency needs with the analytics dashboard's needs and trying to serve both from one store
Not pre-aggregating anything, forcing every analytical query to scan raw event-level data across all shards
keyPoints: Partition/shard by a geography- or entity-based key that matches real query locality, not a high-cardinality key with no locality like trip_id
Maintain pre-aggregated cross-shard rollups so global analytical queries avoid live scatter-gather over every shard
Handle skewed shards (mega-cities) with further sub-partitioning
Separate the low-latency operational/dispatch serving need from the analytical dashboard serving need with different stores
Accept eventual consistency and seconds-level staleness in analytics rollups as a reasonable tradeoff for query speed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ingestion/partitioning key design with sound locality reasoning
Correct sharding strategy and skew-handling approach
Correct cross-shard rollup and serving-layer design

questions.title: When an Indexed View Is Worth the Write Cost
questions.prompt: Your reporting dashboard runs an aggregation query against Production.Product (grouped by subcategory, computing a row count and total list price) hundreds of times per minute during business hours, and the underlying table is only touched by a handful of transactions a day. A teammate suggests materializing this aggregation as an indexed view. Walk through the real requirements for making that work, what SQL Server does differently once it's in place, and the ongoing cost you're trading for speed. Would you recommend it here -- and would your answer change if the table instead took thousands of writes per second?
questions.modelAnswer:
A regular view is just stored SQL text -- it re-runs its underlying SELECT every time it's queried. An indexed view is the one case where that's not true: once you create a unique clustered index on the view, SQL Server physically materializes the computed result set on disk, and queries against the view (or, on Enterprise edition, queries against the base table that the optimizer recognizes as equivalent) can read that pre-computed data directly instead of re-aggregating Production.Product every time.

Getting there has real, non-negotiable requirements: the view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, which locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays consistent with it -- you can't ALTER a schemabound table's referenced columns without dropping dependent objects first. Aggregations must use COUNT_BIG(*), not COUNT(*). A number of T-SQL constructs are disallowed inside the view's definition (TOP, several non-deterministic or imprecise functions, certain outer join shapes). And on non-Enterprise editions, the optimizer won't automatically substitute the indexed view for an equivalent base-table query -- you need the NOEXPAND hint to force it.

The cost is real and ongoing: every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against Production.Product now has to maintain the materialized aggregate too, on top of the base table write. For this scenario -- read-heavy by a wide margin, with only a dozen or so writes a day -- that tradeoff is clearly worth it: you're paying a trivial amount of extra write overhead a handful of times daily to make hundreds of reads per minute avoid re-aggregating the table from scratch. If the table instead took thousands of writes per second, I'd recommend against it: the indexed view's maintenance cost would be paid on every single one of those writes, compounding exactly where you can least afford it, and I'd look at a separate pre-aggregated reporting table refreshed on a schedule, or a different caching layer, instead.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it for the team: a normal view is free to create because it doesn't store anything -- it's just a saved query. An indexed view is different, and the trigger for that difference is adding a unique clustered index to it; the moment you do, SQL Server actually materializes the result on disk. To even get there you need WITH SCHEMABINDING on the view, COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT, and you have to accept that the view's definition is now more restricted -- no TOP, limited function support. And if we're not on Enterprise, I'd flag that the optimizer won't use it automatically; we'd need NOEXPAND in the query, or it just does the full aggregation anyway and we got nothing for the extra complexity.

The real decision point for me is the read/write ratio. In this case we've got maybe a dozen writes a day against hundreds of reads a minute, so I'd absolutely recommend the indexed view -- we're trading a tiny bit of extra work on writes that barely happen for a big win on reads that happen constantly. But if someone told me this table was taking thousands of writes a second, I'd push back hard on the same idea, because now every one of those writes has to keep the materialized aggregate in sync, and that's exactly the kind of hidden cost that tanks throughput on a hot table. In that case I'd rather build a separate summary table refreshed on a schedule, or push the aggregation into a different layer entirely.
questions.example:
CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS ProductCount,
       SUM(ListPrice) AS TotalListPrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;
GO

CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_vw_ProductPriceSummary
ON dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary (ProductSubcategoryID);
GO

-- On Standard edition, force the optimizer to use the materialized data:
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, ProductCount, TotalListPrice
FROM dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary WITH (NOEXPAND);
commonMistakes: Forgetting WITH SCHEMABINDING, which indexed views require
Using COUNT(*) instead of the required COUNT_BIG(*)
Assuming the optimizer auto-uses the indexed view outside Enterprise edition without NOEXPAND
Ignoring write amplification and recommending indexed views for high-write tables
Not accounting for how SCHEMABINDING restricts future ALTER TABLE changes to the base table
keyPoints: Unique clustered index is what actually materializes the view's data
WITH SCHEMABINDING and COUNT_BIG(*) are mandatory requirements
Non-Enterprise editions need the NOEXPAND hint to use the indexed view
Every write to the base table now also maintains the materialized aggregate
Worth it for read-heavy, low-write-ratio reporting aggregations
Not worth it for tables with very high write throughput

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the materialization mechanism and unique clustered index requirement
Names the real requirements (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, restrictions)
Explains the ongoing write-maintenance cost
Gives a correct, justified recommendation for the low-write scenario
Correctly reverses the recommendation for the high-write scenario with reasoning
Mentions NOEXPAND / edition behavior

questions.title: Designing a Reusable Custom Operator for a Recurring Vendor API Extraction
questions.prompt: Six different DAGs each extract data from a different endpoint of the same third-party vendor API (same auth, same pagination style, same rate limits), and each one currently has its own copy-pasted PythonOperator with slightly different retry/backoff logic that's already drifted out of sync. Design a reusable custom operator (or operator + hook pair) architecture that fixes this, and explain what you'd put in the Hook versus the Operator.
questions.modelAnswer:
Split responsibilities the way Airflow's own provider packages do. A VendorApiHook (subclassing BaseHook or HttpHook) owns the connection concerns: reading the shared auth from an Airflow Connection, handling pagination, and rate-limit backoff/retry at the HTTP-call level, exposing a simple method like get_records(endpoint, params) that returns already-paginated, already-authenticated results. A VendorApiExtractOperator (subclassing BaseOperator) owns the task-level concerns: which specific endpoint to call, what to do with the returned records, templated fields for date ranges via Jinja, and Airflow-level retry/on_failure behavior.

The six DAGs then each instantiate VendorApiExtractOperator(endpoint="...", ...) with a few lines of config instead of a bespoke PythonOperator, and a rate-limit or auth fix lands once in the Hook and benefits all six immediately instead of needing six separate PRs. Package this as a small internal Python package (or an airflow_plugins module) so it's versioned and independently testable, with unit tests specifically against the Hook's pagination/backoff logic, since that's the part that drifted and broke trust in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd pull the connection-level stuff -- auth, pagination, rate-limit backoff -- into a Hook, and leave the task-level stuff -- which endpoint, what to do with the records, retries, templated date ranges -- in an Operator that uses that Hook. That's exactly the split Airflow's own provider packages use.

Once that split exists, each of the six DAGs just instantiates the operator with its own endpoint and a few config values, instead of six copy-pasted PythonOperators. And when the rate-limit logic needs a fix, it gets fixed once in the Hook and all six DAGs get the fix automatically instead of six separate PRs that might drift again. I'd package this separately so it's versioned and has its own tests, specifically around the Hook's retry/backoff behavior, since that's the part that's already drifted once.
commonMistakes: Putting HTTP/pagination/retry logic directly in the operator's execute() method instead of a separate Hook, re-coupling connection logic to task logic
Leaving auth/rate-limit handling duplicated across DAGs instead of centralizing it in one Hook
Not versioning the shared Hook/Operator as its own testable package, so fixes still have to be copy-pasted or manually synced
Skipping templated fields, forcing each DAG to hardcode date logic differently
Not writing tests for the Hook's retry/backoff logic specifically, the exact part that drifted and broke trust
keyPoints: Hook owns connection/auth/pagination/rate-limit concerns, reusable across any task
Operator owns task-specific config and Airflow-level behavior (retries, templated fields)
Centralizing shared logic in one Hook means a fix benefits all six DAGs at once
Package and version the Hook/Operator independently so it's testable on its own
This mirrors how Airflow's own provider packages are structured

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct separation of Hook (connection/pagination/rate-limit) vs. Operator (task config/behavior) responsibilities
Explains how centralization fixes the drift problem
Recommends packaging/versioning/testing the shared component
Clear overall explanation

questions.title: Designing Secure Credential Management After a Data Factory Security Audit
questions.prompt: A security audit of your Data Factory environment found linked services with embedded SQL authentication connection strings, including a hardcoded password on one, and a service principal holding Owner on the entire subscription used for Blob Storage access. Design the correct credential and access architecture.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the hardcoded SQL password, the fix is to move it into Azure Key Vault and have the linked service reference it through Key Vault integration rather than storing it in plaintext in the pipeline definition or in any ARM template - that alone makes the credential centrally managed, rotatable, and no longer visible anywhere in source control or deployment artifacts. For the Blob Storage access using an Owner-scoped service principal, I'd go further than just better-hiding that credential: I'd replace it entirely with Data Factory's system-assigned (or user-assigned) managed identity, which removes the need to store or rotate a credential for that connection at all, since Azure handles the identity's authentication behind the scenes.

Whichever identity or service principal remains in use, I'd scope its RBAC role down to exactly what it needs at the narrowest resource boundary that works - Storage Blob Data Contributor on the specific storage account or container it actually touches, never Owner at the subscription level, which is wildly disproportionate to what a pipeline's data-movement activity actually requires. For SQL access specifically, I'd prefer Azure AD authentication via the managed identity where the target is Azure SQL, or if the source is on-premises SQL Server, I'd make sure the self-hosted integration runtime's own service account is tightly scoped and that whatever credential remains in Key Vault has a defined rotation and expiry policy rather than being set-and-forgotten. I'd close this out by removing the subscription-level Owner service principal entirely once the replacement access is validated, adding diagnostic logging and alerts on Key Vault access and linked-service changes to catch future drift, and scheduling a recurring (e.g., quarterly) access review so this becomes an ongoing control rather than a one-time cleanup following an audit finding.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the hardcoded password, that's the easy part to fix - move it into Key Vault and have the linked service pull it from there, so it's never sitting in plaintext in a pipeline definition or an ARM template again. The Owner-on-the-whole-subscription service principal is the part I'd actually spend more time on, because just hiding that credential better in Key Vault doesn't fix the underlying problem - the access itself is wildly overscoped. I'd replace it with Data Factory's managed identity wherever possible, so there's no stored credential at all for that connection, and then scope whatever RBAC role it actually needs down to the specific storage account, not the entire subscription. For SQL, I'd lean on Azure AD authentication through that same managed identity if it's Azure SQL, and if it's still on-prem, I'd make sure the self-hosted IR's service account and whatever's left in Key Vault has an actual rotation schedule instead of being set once and forgotten. And I wouldn't call this done after one cleanup pass - I'd want diagnostic alerts on Key Vault access and linked-service changes, plus a recurring access review, so this doesn't quietly drift back to where it started.
commonMistakes: Moving the password into Key Vault without also addressing the separately serious issue of subscription-level Owner scope
Not considering managed identity as a way to eliminate stored credentials entirely rather than just hiding them better
Granting a 'safer-sounding' but still overly broad role instead of the specific minimal RBAC role actually needed
Not planning credential rotation or an ongoing access review, treating this as a one-time cleanup
Not addressing authentication specifically for the on-premises SQL Server side
keyPoints: Key Vault-backed linked services eliminate plaintext/embedded credentials
Managed identity eliminates stored credentials for Blob Storage access entirely where supported
Scope RBAC to least privilege at the specific resource level, never subscription-level Owner
Prefer Azure AD authentication for SQL where possible
Establish ongoing credential rotation and periodic access review, not a one-time fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes Key Vault integration for remaining credentials
Proposes managed identity to eliminate stored credentials where possible
Correctly scopes RBAC to least privilege
Addresses ongoing rotation/review process
Clarity

questions.title: Structuring External Locations and Storage Credentials Across Dev/Staging/Prod
questions.prompt: Design the Unity Catalog external location and storage credential structure for a platform with three environments (dev, staging, prod), each needing its own storage account, where data engineers should be able to register new external tables in dev freely but need an explicit grant to do so in prod. Walk through how you'd structure the catalogs, external locations, storage credentials, and the permission boundary between environments.
questions.modelAnswer:
The environment boundary should be enforced at every layer, not just one -- catalog, external location, and storage credential should all be environment-specific, so there's no single misconfiguration that lets a dev identity touch prod storage. I'd create three catalogs -- dev, staging, prod -- each mapped to its own storage account rather than three schemas inside one shared catalog, because catalog is the real isolation boundary in Unity Catalog's model and it's also the natural place to scope broad grants like CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE.

Each environment gets its own storage credential object (a managed identity or service principal scoped to that environment's storage account only) and its own external location built on top of that credential, pointing at that environment's container. Critically, the storage credential for prod should not exist in any form that dev or staging identities can reference -- Unity Catalog's CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL and CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION privileges themselves should be restricted to platform admins, not handed to individual data engineers, so engineers are working with external locations that already exist rather than creating new ones that might point somewhere unintended.

For the permission boundary itself: on the dev catalog, grant the data engineering group CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE directly on the dev external location (or on the catalog, inherited down), so anyone on the team can freely register new external tables there without a ticket -- that's the point of dev being a low-friction sandbox. On the prod catalog's external location, don't grant CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE broadly at all; instead, require it as an explicit, individually reviewed grant (or route table creation through a reviewed CI/CD pipeline running as a dedicated service principal with that grant, rather than any human identity having it directly), so every new table that lands in prod storage was deliberately approved rather than something any engineer could do ad hoc. Staging sits in between -- typically grantable to a smaller, trusted subset of the team rather than everyone, mirroring prod's review posture but with lower stakes.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd want the environment boundary enforced at every level, not just one, so there's no single mistake that lets something meant for dev touch prod data. That means three separate catalogs -- dev, staging, prod -- each backed by its own storage account, and each with its own storage credential and external location built specifically for that environment. I wouldn't let any identity, especially an engineer's day-to-day account, hold the privilege to create storage credentials or external locations themselves -- that stays with platform admins, so engineers are always working against infrastructure that already exists and was deliberately set up, not something they can point anywhere on the fly.

On the actual permission split: dev should be low-friction on purpose, so I'd grant the whole data engineering group CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the dev external location directly -- nobody should need to file a ticket to register a new table in a sandbox. Prod is the opposite: I wouldn't hand that grant out broadly at all. Either it's an individually reviewed, named grant for the rare case a human genuinely needs it, or -- what I'd actually push for -- table creation in prod goes through a CI/CD pipeline running as its own service principal that holds the grant, so every new prod table was the result of a reviewed deployment, not an ad hoc CREATE TABLE someone ran from a notebook. Staging I'd treat as the middle ground -- a smaller trusted group, closer to prod's review posture, but without prod's full weight.
commonMistakes: Using schemas within a single shared catalog to separate environments instead of separate catalogs with separate storage
Letting individual engineers hold the privilege to create storage credentials or external locations themselves
Granting CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE broadly on prod the same way it's granted on dev, defeating the review boundary
Reusing the same storage credential or service principal across more than one environment
keyPoints: Separate catalogs per environment, each backed by its own storage account, credential, and external location
Credential/external-location creation privileges restricted to platform admins, not individual engineers
Dev grants CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE broadly to the team for low-friction experimentation
Prod restricts that grant to reviewed, individual approval or a CI/CD service principal rather than direct human access

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly structures catalogs/external locations/credentials per environment
Correctly restricts credential/external-location creation to admins
Correctly designs the dev vs. prod CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE permission boundary
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Group-Based Access Control and Dynamic Views at Scale
questions.prompt: A 200-person data org needs row-level restriction (sales reps only see their own region's rows) and column-level masking (only finance sees unmasked SSNs) on a handful of shared gold tables, without maintaining per-user grants. Design the access-control approach using Unity Catalog groups and dynamic views (or row filters/column masks), and explain why per-user grants don't scale here.
questions.modelAnswer:
Per-user grants break down at this scale for a structural reason, not just a volume one: the access rule is a function of attributes (which region a rep belongs to, whether someone's in finance), not of identity itself, and every grant tied directly to a user has to be manually re-created whenever someone joins, leaves, or changes team -- across 200 people and multiple shared tables, that becomes a permissions system nobody fully trusts or audits, because it drifts the moment headcount changes without someone remembering to update every affected grant.

The fix is to push the "who can see what" logic into the groups and the view definition itself, rather than into per-user grants. I'd set up Unity Catalog groups mirroring the real organizational structure that actually drives access -- one group per sales region, a separate finance group -- and have those group memberships synced from the identity provider (Azure AD/Entra) rather than managed by hand in Databricks, so the source of truth for "who's in region X" lives in one place and access just follows it automatically.

For row-level restriction, I'd implement a row filter function on the gold table that checks is_account_group_member() against the current user's group and compares it to the row's region column, rather than filtering in application code -- it's enforced at the table level so it applies no matter what tool or notebook queries the table. For column masking, a column mask function on the SSN column checks is_account_group_member('finance') and returns the real value only for finance members, masking (redacting, hashing, or nulling) it for everyone else. The key property that makes this scale is that the entire rule lives in one function definition per table, referencing groups rather than individuals -- onboarding a new sales rep to the right region, or moving a rep between regions, is just a group membership change synced from the IdP, with zero changes needed to the table's grants or its row filter/column mask logic.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The core problem with per-user grants here is that the actual rule isn't about who someone is, it's about what group they belong to -- their region, or whether they're in finance -- and the moment you encode that as individual grants, you've built a system that silently goes stale every time someone changes teams or a new hire joins, because nobody remembers to update every grant on every table.

What I'd actually build is group-driven: sync Unity Catalog groups from Azure AD so each sales region has a group and finance has a group, with membership managed where it already lives -- the identity provider -- not hand-maintained inside Databricks. Then the restriction logic goes into the table itself, not into grants on individual people. A row filter function checks which region group the querying user belongs to and only returns rows matching that region; a column mask function checks whether they're in the finance group and only then returns the real SSN value, masking it otherwise. Both are defined once per table and referenced against groups, so when a rep moves from the Midwest region to Northeast, that's a group membership change in the IdP -- nothing about the table's grants, row filter, or column mask needs to change at all. That's really the whole point: the access logic scales with org structure instead of growing linearly with headcount.
commonMistakes: Proposing per-user grants or per-user view copies that require manual maintenance as headcount changes
Implementing row/column restrictions in application or BI-tool logic instead of enforcing them at the table level
Managing group membership by hand inside Databricks instead of syncing it from the identity provider
Writing a separate row filter or mask function per region instead of one function parameterized against group membership
keyPoints: Per-user grants don't scale because the real access rule depends on group attributes, not identity, and drifts as headcount changes
Groups synced from the identity provider become the single source of truth for region/finance membership
A single row filter function per table checks group membership against the row's region column
A single column mask function per table checks finance group membership to reveal or redact SSNs
Access changes become group membership changes, requiring zero changes to table grants or filter/mask logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why per-user grants don't scale for this requirement
Correctly designs group-based row filtering by region
Correctly designs group-based column masking for SSNs
Identifies syncing groups from the identity provider as the maintainable source of truth

questions.title: Row- and Column-Level Security for a Multi-Tenant SaaS Table
questions.prompt: You have a single shared customer_events table in Unity Catalog serving multiple tenant companies, each of whose analysts should only query their own tenant's rows, and a sensitive email column that only that tenant's admins should see unmasked. Design the row filter and column mask approach, and explain what happens if a tenant's analyst writes a query that joins this table against another unfiltered table.
questions.modelAnswer:
The row filter function on customer_events needs to resolve the querying user's tenant and compare it against the row's tenant_id column -- typically by looking up the current user in a small, centrally governed tenant_membership mapping table (user or group to tenant_id) and returning true only when that mapping matches the row's tenant_id, rather than trying to encode tenant membership into Unity Catalog group names directly, since the number of tenants can grow dynamically without needing a new group provisioned for each one. That row filter is attached once, on the table itself, so it applies identically no matter what tool, notebook, or SQL warehouse issues the query.

The column mask on email works the same way structurally but for a narrower population: it checks whether the current user is in that row's tenant's admin mapping (not just any member of the tenant), and returns the real email only for that match, returning a masked/redacted value otherwise -- so a regular analyst within the correct tenant still sees their own tenant's rows, just with email obscured, while that tenant's admin sees it unmasked.

The join behavior is the part people most often get wrong: a row filter is enforced on customer_events itself, at the storage/query-planning layer, regardless of how the table is referenced in a larger query -- so if a tenant's analyst joins customer_events against another, unfiltered table, Unity Catalog still applies the row filter to customer_events's side of the join before the join executes. The analyst only ever sees their own tenant's rows from customer_events in the joined output; rows from other tenants are filtered out before they'd even be available to match against the other table. The real risk isn't that the filter gets bypassed -- it reliably doesn't -- it's if the other, unfiltered table itself contains tenant-identifying or sensitive data without its own protection, in which case the join can still leak that table's own unprotected columns, which is a property of the other table's access control, not a hole in customer_events's row filter.
questions.professionalAnswer:
For the row filter, I wouldn't try to bake tenant membership into Unity Catalog group names one-for-one, because tenants get added dynamically and that'd mean provisioning a new group every time a customer signs up. Instead I'd have the row filter function look up the current user against a small tenant_membership table -- user to tenant_id -- and only return rows where that matches the row's tenant_id. One filter function, attached to the table once, works for every tenant without needing per-tenant configuration.

Column masking on email works the same shape but checks a narrower condition -- is this user specifically an admin for this row's tenant, not just any member -- and only then returns the real value; everyone else gets it masked, including regular analysts inside the correct tenant.

The join question is the one people get nervous about, but the row filter doesn't care how the table is referenced -- it's enforced on customer_events itself before the join even happens, so a tenant's analyst joining it against some other table still only ever sees their own tenant's rows from customer_events in the result. What I would actually worry about is the other table in that join: if it has its own tenant-sensitive columns and isn't separately protected, the join can leak that table's data just fine -- that's not a hole in customer_events's filter, that's a gap in the other table's own access control that needs its own fix.
commonMistakes: Trying to encode tenant membership as a Unity Catalog group per tenant instead of a lookup table, which doesn't scale as tenants grow
Assuming a row filter can be bypassed or weakened by joining the filtered table against another table
Confusing tenant-membership masking (any tenant member) with tenant-admin masking (only admins) for the email column
Overlooking that an unfiltered second table in the join can still leak its own sensitive data independent of the first table's protection
keyPoints: Row filter resolves the current user's tenant via a membership lookup, not per-tenant groups, and compares it to tenant_id
Column mask on email checks tenant-admin membership specifically, narrower than general tenant membership
Row filters are enforced on the protected table itself regardless of how it's joined, so tenant isolation holds across joins
A join can still leak data if the other table involved has its own unprotected sensitive columns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the tenant row filter approach
Correctly designs the tenant-admin column mask on email
Correctly explains row filter enforcement across joins
Identifies the real residual risk (the other table's own protection)
