questions.title: Sharing a Gold Table with an External Partner Without Copying Data
questions.prompt: A retail partner needs read access to your gold-layer inventory table, refreshed daily, but you don't want to give them a copy of the data, a service principal in your account, or a standing SQL endpoint they query directly. Design a Delta Sharing approach for this, and explain what the partner actually receives and how their access differs depending on whether they're a Databricks-to-Databricks recipient or not.
questions.modelAnswer:
Delta Sharing fits exactly because it separates "granting access to data" from "copying data" or "granting access to your compute." I'd create a share object containing the gold inventory table (or a view over it, if the partner should only see a filtered or column-reduced subset rather than the full table), and add the partner as a recipient on that share. No service principal in your account, no SQL endpoint exposed to them, and no file copy -- the share is just a governed pointer to the existing Delta table's current state, enforced through Unity Catalog's grant model the same way any other object is.

What the partner actually receives depends entirely on whether they're a Databricks-to-Databricks recipient (meaning their own account is also on Unity Catalog) or an open recipient (meaning they're not on Databricks, or you don't want to depend on them being so). For a Databricks-to-Databricks recipient, you share directly to their Unity Catalog metastore identifier, and the shared table shows up in their own workspace as a Unity Catalog object -- they can read it with Spark, SQL, or any Databricks-native tool, with the same governance semantics (grants, lineage visibility into it being a shared object) as any other catalog object in their account, and they never get credentials to your storage. For an open recipient, you instead generate a bearer-token-based activation link and a credential file -- the open sharing protocol -- and they read the table through any Delta Sharing-compatible client (pandas/Spark connectors exist outside Databricks too, including Power BI and other BI tools with native connectors), authenticated by that token rather than by being a known identity in your account at all.

Either way, "refreshed daily" just falls out of the share pointing at the live table -- there's no separate export or sync step to maintain; the moment your own gold table updates, the next read through the share reflects the new state, and you can revoke the recipient's access at any time without having to claw back a copy that already left your environment.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Delta Sharing is really built for exactly this shape of problem -- you want someone to read your data without you ever handing them a copy of it, a login into your account, or a standing endpoint they can hit whenever. I'd create a share wrapping the gold inventory table, trim it down to a view if there's anything in there the partner shouldn't see, and add them as a recipient -- that's the whole mechanism, no credentials into your storage, no account access.

What they actually get back depends on whether they're on Databricks themselves. If they are, and we set it up Databricks-to-Databricks, the shared table just shows up as a catalog object inside their own Unity Catalog metastore -- they query it like any other table they have, through their own tools, and they never see your infrastructure at all. If they're not on Databricks -- open sharing -- we hand them an activation link and a credential file instead, and they read the table through a Delta Sharing client, which plenty of BI tools and even plain pandas/Spark support now, authenticated by that token rather than by being a recognized identity in our account.

And the daily refresh part basically takes care of itself -- the share just points at the live table, so the moment it updates, the next read sees the new data. No export job to maintain, and if the partnership ever ends, we revoke the recipient and that's it -- there's no copy sitting out there we have to go track down and ask them to delete.
commonMistakes: Proposing to export/copy the table to a location the partner can access instead of using a live share
Creating a service principal or workspace account for the partner rather than a Delta Sharing recipient
Assuming all external recipients need to be on Databricks to receive a share
Forgetting that a share can expose a filtered/reduced view rather than the full underlying table
keyPoints: Delta Sharing grants access to a live table/view via a share and recipient, without copying data or granting account access
Databricks-to-Databricks recipients see the shared object natively in their own Unity Catalog metastore
Open recipients authenticate via a token/credential file using any Delta Sharing-compatible client
The share reflects the live table's current state, so daily refresh requires no separate export or sync step
Access can be revoked at any time since no copy of the data left the environment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the share/recipient approach without copying data or granting account access
Correctly explains Databricks-to-Databricks recipient access
Correctly explains open/non-Databricks recipient access
Correctly explains why daily refresh requires no extra sync step

questions.title: Choosing Between Auto Loader, COPY INTO, and a Partner Ingestion Tool
questions.prompt: You're ingesting three different sources into a Databricks lakehouse: a high-volume continuous stream of IoT sensor files landing every few seconds, a nightly batch drop of a few hundred CSV files from a partner's SFTP export, and a transactional database that needs CDC-style change capture. Walk through which ingestion approach you'd pick for each and why a one-size-fits-all choice (e.g., Auto Loader for everything) would be wrong for at least one of them.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the IoT sensor stream, Auto Loader in streaming mode with file notifications is the right fit, and it's the clearest case of the three: the volume and continuous arrival pattern are exactly what Auto Loader's incremental, event-driven file discovery is built for, and running it as a genuine Structured Streaming job (rather than a scheduled batch trigger) keeps latency low without the overhead of repeatedly listing a directory that's constantly getting new files.

For the nightly batch of a few hundred partner CSVs from SFTP, Auto Loader would be defensible but is more machinery than the problem needs -- a few hundred files once a night doesn't need incremental streaming infrastructure, checkpointing, or a long-running cluster. COPY INTO is the better fit here: it's an idempotent, SQL-native batch load that tracks which files it's already loaded, runs as a simple scheduled job against a cluster that spins up, loads, and shuts down, and doesn't carry streaming state or a checkpoint location that outlives the job the way Auto Loader does. For a small, regular batch drop, that simplicity is a real advantage, not a limitation.

For the transactional database needing CDC, neither Auto Loader nor COPY INTO is the right tool at all, because both operate on files landing in storage, and a live transactional database isn't producing files -- it's producing row-level inserts/updates/deletes inside its own engine. That needs an actual CDC mechanism: either a native database change-feed/log-based capture tool (e.g., a managed CDC connector, or Debezium-style log tailing) that extracts changes and writes them somewhere Databricks can consume, with Delta Lake's MERGE INTO (or Lakeflow's native CDC/APPLY CHANGES support) applying those captured changes to the target table idempotently. Treating this like a file-ingestion problem and trying to force Auto Loader onto periodic full-table exports would mean losing true change history (you'd only ever see full snapshots, not what specifically changed and when) and paying for repeatedly re-reading the entire table instead of just the deltas -- which is exactly the one-size-fits-all mistake: Auto Loader excels at file arrival, not at database change capture, and using it there either doesn't work or quietly reinvents CDC badly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd pick three different tools here on purpose, because these aren't actually the same problem wearing different clothes. The IoT stream is the easy one -- continuous, high-volume file arrival is literally what Auto Loader with file notifications is built for, run as a real streaming job so latency stays low instead of batching it on a schedule.

The nightly SFTP batch is where I'd actually push back on using Auto Loader even though it could technically do the job -- a few hundred files once a night doesn't need streaming infrastructure, checkpoints, and a long-running job to manage. COPY INTO is simpler and exactly sized for this: SQL-native, idempotent, tracks what it's already loaded, and the cluster just spins up, does the load, and goes away. No reason to carry streaming machinery for something that happens once a day.

The database CDC case is where a one-size-fits-all choice would actually break, not just be overkill. Auto Loader and COPY INTO both assume files landing in storage -- a live transactional database isn't producing files, it's producing row-level changes inside its own engine. Trying to force file-based ingestion onto that, say by periodically exporting full snapshots, means you lose the actual change history -- you only ever see "what the table looks like now," not what specifically changed -- and you're re-reading the whole table every time instead of just the deltas. That needs a real CDC tool, log-based or connector-based, feeding into something like MERGE INTO or Lakeflow's native change-apply support, because that's the only approach that actually captures row-level change, which is the whole point of CDC in the first place.
commonMistakes: Using Auto Loader for the nightly batch instead of a simpler, idempotent batch tool like COPY INTO
Trying to force Auto Loader or COPY INTO onto the database CDC case by scheduling periodic full-table exports
Not recognizing that CDC requires row-level change capture, which file-based ingestion tools cannot provide on their own
Assuming one ingestion tool should be used everywhere for consistency, regardless of each source's actual arrival pattern
keyPoints: Auto Loader fits the continuous, high-volume file-arrival pattern of the IoT stream
COPY INTO is the better-sized, simpler idempotent batch tool for a modest nightly file drop
Database CDC requires a genuine change-capture mechanism, not file-based ingestion, since there are no files to discover
Forcing file-based tools onto CDC loses true change history and forces repeated full-table reads

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches Auto Loader to the IoT streaming scenario
Correctly matches COPY INTO to the nightly batch scenario with justification
Correctly identifies that CDC requires a different mechanism entirely
Clearly explains why a one-size-fits-all choice fails for at least one source

questions.title: Orchestrating a Multi-Step Pipeline That Fans Out and Back In
questions.prompt: Design a Databricks Workflow where a single upstream Lakeflow pipeline run needs to trigger four independent downstream notebook tasks that each build a different gold aggregate table, followed by one final task that only runs after all four succeed and sends a completion signal to a downstream team. Walk through how you'd structure the task dependency graph and handle the case where exactly one of the four downstream tasks fails.
questions.modelAnswer:
The dependency graph has a fan-out point and a fan-in point, and both need to be modeled explicitly rather than assumed. The Lakeflow pipeline runs as its own task (a pipeline task type, not a notebook task) at the top of the graph. Each of the four gold-aggregate notebook tasks declares depends_on pointing at that pipeline task -- not at each other -- so all four become independent, parallel branches that start as soon as the pipeline task succeeds, rather than running sequentially. The final notify_downstream task then declares depends_on against all four aggregate tasks simultaneously; Databricks Workflows' default dependency semantics require every listed dependency to succeed before a task is eligible to run, which is exactly the fan-in behavior needed here -- the notification only fires once all four gold tables are genuinely built, not after just one or some of them.

For the case where exactly one of the four fails: by default, a task whose dependency fails doesn't run, so notify_downstream would simply never execute, and the job as a whole reports as failed -- which correctly reflects that the downstream team shouldn't be told "data's ready" when one of the four gold tables isn't. The three successful aggregate tasks still completed and wrote their tables; only the notification is (correctly) withheld. The one failing task should carry its own retry policy appropriate to its likely failure mode, and if it's still failing after retries, the job surfaces that specific task's failure in the run view rather than a vague "something failed," so whoever's on call can go straight to the one broken branch instead of auditing all four.

One refinement worth adding deliberately: if partial completion needs to be communicated too (e.g., the downstream team can start consuming the three tables that did succeed while the fourth is being fixed), that's a conscious design choice -- either a separate task with run_if: at_least_one_success-style conditional logic sending a partial-completion notice, or simply leaving it as an all-or-nothing gate and accepting that the downstream team waits for full completion. That's a product decision about what "done" means to the consuming team, not something the orchestration model forces either way.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd model this as a clean fan-out, fan-in shape rather than trying to get clever. The Lakeflow pipeline is its own task at the top. All four gold-aggregate notebook tasks list that pipeline task as their one dependency -- not each other -- so Workflows kicks all four off in parallel the moment the pipeline succeeds, instead of running them one after another for no reason. Then the notify task lists all four aggregate tasks as its dependencies, and Workflows' default behavior is that every single one of those has to succeed before the notify task is even eligible to run -- which is exactly the fan-in gate I want, since I never want a "data's ready" signal going out when only three of four tables actually built.

If exactly one of the four fails, here's what actually happens without me doing anything special: the notify task just never runs, because one of its dependencies didn't succeed, and the overall job shows as failed. The other three aggregate tasks still finished and their tables are sitting there built correctly -- it's only the final notification that's correctly withheld. I'd make sure the failing task has its own sensible retry policy, and if it keeps failing after that, the job run view points straight at that one task, so whoever's debugging doesn't have to go hunting across all four.

The one thing I'd flag as a real decision, not something the tool decides for me: if the downstream team would actually benefit from knowing three of four tables are ready while the fourth gets fixed, that's a separate conditional task I'd have to build on purpose -- the default all-succeed gate doesn't give me partial notification for free, and I wouldn't want to build that without first checking whether the downstream team actually wants partial signals or would rather just wait for all four.
commonMistakes: Chaining the four aggregate tasks sequentially instead of having them all depend only on the upstream pipeline task
Assuming the notify task runs automatically after any subset of the four succeeds rather than requiring all four
Not realizing a dependency failure silently skips downstream tasks rather than causing an explicit error on them
Building partial-success notification logic without confirming the downstream team actually wants partial signals

questions.title: Cost-Optimizing a Large Nightly Workload Without Hurting Reliability
questions.prompt: A nightly batch job cluster processing several terabytes is costing significantly more than budgeted, and your VP wants the bill cut by a third without blowing the SLA. Walk through the levers you'd actually evaluate -- cluster sizing/autoscaling, spot/spot-fallback instances, Photon, and caching -- and the order you'd try them in, including which lever you'd be most cautious about given the SLA constraint.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd order these from lowest-risk-to-SLA to highest, because the VP's actual constraint is "cut cost without blowing the SLA," not just "cut cost," so the levers that are nearly free from a reliability standpoint should be tried, and measured, before the ones that introduce new failure modes.

First, Photon: enabling it is close to a free lever for most SQL/DataFrame-heavy workloads -- it's a drop-in vectorized execution engine swap that typically speeds up the same workload meaningfully with no code changes and no new risk to reliability, which both lowers the bill directly (same job finishes faster, consuming less cluster-hours) and buys SLA headroom for other changes. I'd measure its actual impact on this specific workload before assuming a number, since gains vary by workload shape, but it's the right first thing to try precisely because it can't make reliability worse.

Second, right-sizing and autoscaling: review whether the current cluster is oversized for the actual data volume (common after past "just make it bigger" fixes to unrelated problems) and whether autoscaling bounds are tuned to the workload's actual shape rather than a static, conservatively-large fixed size. This is still relatively low-risk if done by actually profiling the job's resource usage rather than guessing, but it needs real profiling data, not an assumption, since undersizing directly risks the SLA.

Third, caching: review whether frequently-reused intermediate results (a lookup table joined repeatedly, a dimension read multiple times across the job) are being recomputed instead of cached, since eliminating redundant recomputation lowers both runtime and cost without changing what the job actually computes.

The lever I'd be most cautious about, and would evaluate last with the most scrutiny, is spot instances. Spot/spot-with-fallback can meaningfully cut compute cost, but it introduces a genuinely new failure mode -- instance reclamation mid-job -- that didn't exist before, and for a nightly job with a hard SLA, an eviction at the wrong moment is exactly the kind of risk the VP explicitly asked me not to take on. If I use spot at all, it would be with on-demand fallback configured and only after the other levers have already closed most of the cost gap, so spot is covering a smaller remaining slice of the workload rather than carrying the SLA-critical path alone.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd order these by how much new risk they introduce to the SLA, since that's really the constraint here, not just "make it cheaper." Photon goes first -- for most of this kind of workload it's close to a free win, a vectorized engine swap with no code changes, and it directly helps both cost and SLA headroom since the same job just finishes faster. I'd actually measure it on this workload rather than assume a number, but it's the safest thing to try and it buys me room before I touch anything riskier.

Next I'd look at whether the cluster's actually sized right -- a lot of these "cut the bill" asks trace back to a cluster that got oversized at some point for an unrelated reason and never got revisited, or autoscaling bounds set conservatively high out of caution rather than actual profiling. That's still fairly low-risk as long as I'm profiling real usage, not guessing, since getting it wrong in the other direction risks the SLA directly.

Then caching -- if there's a lookup or dimension table getting recomputed repeatedly across the job instead of cached once, that's free savings with basically no downside.

The one I'd save for last, and be genuinely careful with, is spot instances. They can cut compute cost meaningfully, but they come with a real new risk -- the cloud provider can reclaim the instance mid-job -- and for a job with a hard SLA, that's exactly the kind of risk I don't want to introduce casually. If I use spot at all, it's with on-demand fallback configured, and only after the safer levers have already closed most of the gap, so spot's only covering a smaller slice of the job rather than being load-bearing for the SLA.
commonMistakes: Reaching for spot instances first because it looks like the biggest cost lever, without accounting for the eviction risk to the SLA
Right-sizing the cluster by guessing instead of profiling actual resource usage on the real workload
Assuming Photon's speedup without measuring it on the specific workload, since gains vary by workload shape
Treating cost-cutting and SLA risk as independent concerns instead of ordering levers by their actual risk to the SLA
keyPoints: Photon is evaluated first as a near-free lever with minimal reliability risk
Right-sizing and autoscaling tuning should be based on actual profiling, not guesswork
Caching eliminates redundant recomputation of reused intermediate results
Spot instances are evaluated last and most cautiously, since they introduce real eviction risk to a hard SLA

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly evaluates and sequences all four levers
Justifies the sequencing by actual risk to the SLA, not just cost impact
Correctly identifies spot instances as the highest-risk lever given the SLA constraint
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a Secrets Management Scheme for Multi-Team Pipelines
questions.prompt: Several teams' Databricks pipelines need credentials for external systems (a third-party API key, a database connection string, a service principal secret), and you want to avoid both hardcoded credentials in notebooks and a single shared secret scope every team has equal access to. Design the secret scope structure, explain the difference between a Databricks-backed scope and an Azure Key Vault-backed scope, and when you'd choose one over the other.
questions.modelAnswer:
The structural fix for "one shared scope, equal access for everyone" is to scope secrets per team (or per system, when a credential is genuinely shared across teams) rather than pooling everything into one scope, and to attach ACLs to each scope so only the group that actually needs a given credential can read it -- a secrets architecture should mirror the organizational boundary of who needs what, not just centralize secrets for convenience. I'd create one scope per team for team-owned credentials (e.g., team-marketing-secrets holding that team's third-party API key) and separate, narrowly-scoped shared scopes for genuinely cross-team systems (e.g., a shared-db-secrets scope for a database several teams' pipelines connect to), with READ granted only to the specific groups that need that specific scope -- never a blanket grant across all scopes to all engineers.

A Databricks-backed secret scope stores the secret's encrypted value inside Databricks' own secret store, managed entirely through the Databricks CLI/API/UI; it's simple to set up, requires no external dependency, and is a reasonable default for secrets that only need to exist inside Databricks and aren't already managed somewhere else. An Azure Key Vault-backed scope is different in an important way: it doesn't store the secret in Databricks at all -- it's a reference to a secret that actually lives in an Azure Key Vault instance, so Databricks is reading through to a vault that likely already has its own access policies, rotation automation, and audit logging, and is probably already the system of record other non-Databricks applications use for the same credential.

I'd choose Key Vault-backed scopes whenever the credential either needs to be shared with non-Databricks systems (so there's one real source of truth instead of two copies that can drift), needs automated rotation (Key Vault's rotation policies apply to the actual secret, not a copy sitting in Databricks), or falls under a compliance requirement that already mandates centralizing secrets in Key Vault. I'd use Databricks-backed scopes for secrets that are genuinely Databricks-only and don't need that extra infrastructure -- the added indirection of a Key Vault-backed scope isn't worth it for something no other system will ever touch.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The structural problem with one shared scope is that it bakes in equal access by construction -- everyone with access to the scope has access to every secret in it, regardless of whether their pipeline actually needs that particular credential. So I'd split it along the lines of who actually needs what: one scope per team for that team's own credentials, and a handful of narrowly scoped shared scopes for the credentials that genuinely cross team lines, with ACLs granting READ only to the groups that specifically need each scope -- not a blanket grant across everything to every engineer.

On the Databricks-backed versus Key Vault-backed question: a Databricks-backed scope just stores the encrypted secret inside Databricks itself -- simple, no external dependency, fine for something that's genuinely Databricks-only. A Key Vault-backed scope is different in a way that actually matters -- it's not storing the secret at all, it's a pointer into an Azure Key Vault where the real secret lives, which usually means that secret already has its own rotation policy, its own access controls, and its own audit trail, and probably other non-Databricks systems are already reading the same secret from the same vault.

That's exactly when I'd reach for Key Vault-backed: when the credential is shared outside Databricks, when it needs real rotation automation, or when there's already a compliance requirement that secrets live in Key Vault as the single source of truth. If it's something only Databricks will ever touch and nothing else needs it, I wouldn't bother with the extra indirection -- a Databricks-backed scope is simpler and perfectly appropriate there.
commonMistakes: Keeping one shared secret scope with broad access instead of scoping per team and attaching narrow ACLs
Assuming Databricks-backed and Key Vault-backed scopes are functionally interchangeable with no real tradeoff
Choosing Key Vault-backed scopes universally without considering the added indirection for secrets that are genuinely Databricks-only
Not accounting for rotation and cross-system reuse when deciding where a credential's source of truth should live
keyPoints: Secret scopes should mirror organizational boundaries, with per-team scopes and narrow ACLs rather than one shared scope
Databricks-backed scopes store the secret's encrypted value inside Databricks itself
Key Vault-backed scopes reference a secret whose real source of truth lives in Azure Key Vault
Key Vault-backed scopes are preferred when the credential is shared outside Databricks, needs rotation, or has a compliance requirement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs scoped secret structure with per-team/per-system ACLs
Correctly explains the mechanical difference between Databricks-backed and Key Vault-backed scopes
Correctly identifies when to choose Key Vault-backed vs. Databricks-backed scopes
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Moving a Portal-Clicking Team to Terraform/Bicep Over Skeptical Senior Pushback
questions.prompt: Your team has always provisioned Azure resources by clicking through the portal, and you want to move the team to Terraform/Bicep for a new data platform build. Two senior teammates are skeptical, citing 'it's slower than just clicking the thing I need' and past frustration with a previous team's over-engineered Terraform setup. How do you negotiate this adoption?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats the skepticism as legitimate signal rather than resistance to be overcome by mandate. The candidate should start by separating the two objections, since they need different responses: 'portal is faster for a one-off' is often true and should be acknowledged honestly rather than argued away, while the past bad experience with over-engineered Terraform is a real scar that a new rollout needs to explicitly design against -- by keeping the initial module set small, flat, and genuinely necessary rather than building abstraction layers nobody asked for.

The candidate should propose an approach that lets the skeptics experience the value rather than being told about it: start with a new, lower-stakes piece of the platform build, let the team keep clicking for genuinely one-off exploratory resources for now, and bring the skeptics into writing the first modules rather than handing them a framework decided in isolation. The real argument for adoption -- consistent, reviewable, repeatable environments; drift detection; faster disaster recovery -- should be made concretely against this specific platform build's needs, not as an abstract best-practice argument, and the candidate should be honest that there's a real short-term velocity cost that pays off over the project's lifetime, not instantly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't go in trying to win an argument -- I'd go in treating their pushback as two separate, legitimate points that need different answers. 'Clicking is faster for the thing I need right now' is just true a lot of the time, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But 'the last Terraform setup I used was over-engineered and painful' is the one I actually need to address head-on, by being explicit that whatever we build this time starts small and flat -- no module-of-modules, no abstraction for things we don't have yet.

Practically, I'd rather let them feel the benefit than argue them into it. I'd pick a lower-stakes piece of the new platform build to go first, keep it genuinely simple, and actually have the two of them help write those first modules instead of handing them something I designed alone and asking them to adopt it. And I'd be straight with them that yes, this is going to be a bit slower than clicking for the first few weeks -- the payoff is in repeatable environments and not having to remember what we clicked six months from now when we need to rebuild something, and that's a real tradeoff, not a free win I'm selling them.
commonMistakes: Treating the skepticism as pure resistance to change instead of partially valid feedback
Arguing that Terraform is strictly faster, which isn't true for small one-off changes and damages credibility
Ignoring or dismissing the team's past bad experience with an over-engineered IaC setup instead of designing against it
Mandating the switch top-down without letting the skeptics co-author the first real modules
Overselling adoption as a free win instead of being honest about the short-term velocity cost
keyPoints: Separates the 'portal is faster' objection from the 'past over-engineering' objection and addresses each specifically
Explicitly designs the new rollout to be small and simple, directly countering the past bad experience
Lets skeptics experience the value on a real, lower-stakes piece of work rather than mandating from above
Involves the skeptical senior teammates in authoring the first modules
Is honest about the real short-term velocity tradeoff rather than overselling adoption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates and responds to the two distinct objections
Proposes a concrete plan to avoid repeating the past over-engineering experience
Involves the skeptical teammates directly rather than mandating adoption top-down
Makes a concrete, project-specific case for adoption rather than an abstract best-practices argument
Is honest about real tradeoffs instead of overselling the change

questions.title: Leading a Blameless Postmortem on a Terraform Apply That Took Down a Shared Event Hub
questions.prompt: A `terraform apply` run by a teammate, approved in a rushed review, took down a shared production Event Hub namespace for 40 minutes before anyone noticed. You're leading the blameless postmortem. How do you run it so it's genuinely blameless but still produces real accountability and fixes?
questions.modelAnswer:
Blameless does not mean avoiding naming what happened -- the postmortem should state plainly that a specific Terraform change, approved in a rushed review, triggered the outage, while keeping the framing on the system that allowed it rather than on the individuals as people. The candidate should reframe the central question from 'who broke the Event Hub' to 'what let a plan with this blast radius get approved in a rushed review, and why did it take 40 minutes to notice a shared production namespace was down.' That reframing is what produces durable fixes instead of two people -- the author and the reviewer -- feeling punished while the same gap exists for the next risky change.

The candidate should explicitly involve both the author and the reviewer in walking through their reasoning: what the plan output looked like, what time pressure existed, why the blast radius of the change (a shared resource used by other teams) wasn't flagged in review. The postmortem should close with concrete, owned, dated action items distinct from the individuals' behavior -- for example, requiring plan output to explicitly call out changes to shared/cross-team resources, a mandatory second reviewer or cooling-off period for changes touching shared infrastructure, and alerting on the Event Hub namespace's health so a future outage is caught in minutes, not 40.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Blameless doesn't mean we're vague about what happened -- I'll say directly that a specific apply, approved in a review that got rushed, is what took the namespace down. But I keep steering the room toward the system question: what let a change with this big a blast radius get approved quickly, and why did it take 40 minutes before anyone noticed a shared production resource was gone, rather than who personally messed up.

I'd ask both the person who wrote the change and the person who reviewed it to actually walk through their side -- what the plan output showed, what the time pressure looked like, whether anything flagged that this touched a resource other teams depend on. And I'm not going to let the meeting end as just a good conversation -- I want it to end with specific fixes: plan output that calls out changes to shared resources explicitly, maybe a required second reviewer or a short cooling-off window for anything touching shared infra, and health alerting on that namespace so next time we catch it in minutes instead of 40.
commonMistakes: Conflating 'blameless' with being vague about what actually happened or who was involved
Focusing on the individual author's or reviewer's judgment instead of the systemic review gap
Not inviting both the author and the reviewer to explain their actual context and reasoning
Treating the 40-minute detection delay as a footnote instead of an equally important separate finding
Ending with a narrative discussion but no concrete, owned, dated action items
keyPoints: States plainly what happened and who was involved without making it about individual blame
Reframes toward the systemic gap: why a high-blast-radius change cleared a rushed review
Involves both the author and reviewer constructively to surface real context
Treats the 40-minute detection delay as its own distinct, important finding
Closes with concrete, owned, dated action items covering both the review gap and detection gap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Distinguishes blameless from avoiding naming the actual cause and people involved
Reframes the discussion toward the systemic review gap rather than individual fault
Involves both author and reviewer constructively to surface context, not blame
Identifies the detection delay as a separate, equally important finding
Produces concrete, owned, dated action items addressing both gaps

questions.title: Handling a Skeptical Interviewer's Challenge Mid-Whiteboard on Your Own Real Design
questions.prompt: You're in a final-round interview loop and asked to whiteboard the system design for a real-time analytics platform you actually built at a previous job. Partway through, the interviewer challenges a tradeoff you made, somewhat skeptically. How do you handle being challenged on your own real design decision mid-presentation?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats the challenge as a legitimate, even useful, part of the interview rather than a threat to defend against reflexively. The candidate should describe pausing briefly rather than rushing to justify, genuinely considering whether the interviewer has a real point before responding, since a reflexive defense reads as weaker than a considered one even if the final answer is the same.

The response should reconstruct the actual context the decision was made in -- what constraints existed at the time (team size, timeline, existing infrastructure, specific latency or cost requirements), what alternatives were genuinely considered, and why the chosen tradeoff won given those constraints -- rather than asserting the decision was simply correct in the abstract. If the interviewer's challenge points to a real limitation of the original decision, the strongest answer acknowledges it honestly ('that's a fair point -- if I were building this today with different constraints, I'd probably lean X') rather than defending a decision as flawless, since real systems always involve tradeoffs and an interviewer is often testing for intellectual honesty as much as the original technical choice. The candidate should keep the tone collaborative, not adversarial, treating it as a genuine technical discussion rather than a test to be won.
questions.professionalAnswer:
When that happens, my first instinct is to actually pause for a second instead of jumping straight into defending myself, because a considered answer lands a lot better than a reflexive one, even if I end up saying the same thing. I'll genuinely ask myself whether they've spotted something real before I respond.

Then what I try to do is walk them back through the actual constraints we had at the time -- team size, the timeline we were under, what was already in place, the specific latency numbers we had to hit -- and why that tradeoff won given those constraints, rather than just insisting it was the objectively correct call. And honestly, if what they're pointing at is a real limitation, I'll just say so -- something like, 'that's fair, if I were building this today with more time or a different team, I'd probably lean the other way.' I don't think interviewers are looking for someone who thinks their old design was flawless -- I think a lot of them are specifically testing whether I can be challenged on my own work without getting defensive, so I try to treat it like a real conversation about tradeoffs, not a fight I need to win.

Failing to reconstruct the actual constraints that shaped the original decision
Treating the exchange as adversarial rather than a genuine technical discussion
Conceding too quickly without defending a decision that was actually sound given its constraints

Balances honesty about limitations with a genuine defense of sound original reasoning

questions.title: Writing and Estimating User Stories for a BI Deliverable in Sprint Planning
questions.prompt: Your Scrum team is planning the next sprint. Product wants 'a dashboard showing customer lifetime value by region' as a single backlog item, estimated at 3 story points by a junior analyst who hasn't scoped the data sources yet. As the senior BI person on the team, you suspect this is actually multiple stories hiding inside one, with real uncertainty in the CLV calculation logic and an unvalidated data source. How do you handle this in backlog grooming?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer uses backlog grooming to decompose the vague item into independently valuable, estimable stories rather than accepting or silently re-estimating a single large story. The candidate should describe splitting it along natural seams: a story to validate and document the CLV calculation logic with the business stakeholder, a story to confirm and connect the required data sources, a story to build the underlying semantic model/measures, and a story for the dashboard visualization itself — each with its own acceptance criteria.

The candidate should explain why the junior analyst's 3-point estimate was likely too low without undermining them in front of the team: the estimate was made before the unknowns (calculation logic, data source validation) were surfaced, which is a common and correctable planning gap, not a competence failure. A senior team member re-estimates collaboratively, using planning poker or a similar team technique, once the stories are properly split, rather than overriding the estimate unilaterally.

The response should also note the broader behavior being modeled for the team: a senior person makes unknowns visible early in grooming rather than letting the team discover them mid-sprint, and treats precise, honestly-scoped story splitting as part of their responsibility to the sprint's predictability, not just a nice-to-have.
questions.professionalAnswer:
In grooming, I'd just say out loud, 'I don't think this is one story — I think there are at least three stories hiding inside it.' I'd split it: one story to pin down the actual CLV formula with Product, because 'lifetime value' means five different things depending on who you ask; one to confirm the data sources actually have what we need and are joinable; one for the underlying model and measures; and one for the dashboard itself.

I'd be careful not to make the junior analyst feel called out for the 3-point estimate — I'd frame it as, 'this was estimated before we knew about the unknowns in the calculation logic, which is totally normal, that's exactly what grooming is for.' Then I'd have the team re-estimate each piece together once it's split, rather than me just overriding his number myself. Honestly, the biggest thing I'm modeling here for the team is that surfacing unknowns in grooming, before the sprint starts, is a core part of the job — not something you only do when something breaks mid-sprint.

Not surfacing the calculation-logic ambiguity ('lifetime value' meaning) before committing to the sprint
Letting unknowns about data source validity go unaddressed until mid-sprint discovery

questions.title: Justifying a Unity Catalog Governance Design to a Skeptical Security Team
questions.prompt: You've proposed a Unity Catalog permission model built around group-based grants and dynamic views rather than per-user ACLs on every table. Your security team pushes back, saying they want to review and approve access on a per-user, per-table basis for audit purposes. How do you make the case for your design without just overriding their concern?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats the security team's underlying goal -- a reliable, reviewable record of who can see what -- as legitimate and worth preserving, while pushing back specifically on per-user-per-table review as the mechanism, since that mechanism is what won't actually scale or stay accurate, not the goal itself. The candidate should resist framing this as "my design is more elegant," which doesn't address the security team's real concern, and instead show that group-based access produces a clearer audit trail than per-user ACLs would in practice: with groups, "who can access table X" is answered by one group membership list that's synced from the identity provider, versus hundreds of individual grants that drift the moment someone changes teams and nobody remembers to update every affected table.

The candidate should propose a concrete compromise that gives the security team real review power without reverting to per-user ACLs: they review and approve the group definitions and what each group can access (a much smaller, stable surface than per-user grants), and they get visibility into group membership changes as those happen, rather than approving each individual's access to each table one at a time. The candidate should also acknowledge directly that this does shift where human judgment is applied -- review happens at the group/role design level rather than per person -- and should be honest that this requires the security team to trust that group membership itself is being managed correctly, which is a real ask, not something to minimize.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't go in trying to win the argument on "my design is cleaner" -- that's not actually their concern. What they want is a trustworthy answer to "who can see this data," and I think group-based access actually gives them a better version of that, not a worse one, so that's the case I'd make.

With per-user ACLs on every table, the honest reality is that record goes stale constantly -- someone changes teams, and now there's a stale grant on some table nobody remembers to revoke, and "who has access" becomes a question you can't actually answer confidently six months later. With groups synced from the identity provider, "who can access this" is one membership list, and it's accurate because it's the same list driving everything else in the org, not a parallel thing I'm separately maintaining.

So what I'd offer them is: review and sign off on the group definitions and what each group can touch -- a much smaller, more stable thing to review than hundreds of per-user grants -- and get visibility into membership changes as they happen. That's real oversight, just applied at a different layer. And I'd be straight with them that this does mean trusting that group membership itself is managed correctly, which is a real thing to ask of them, not something I'd want to wave away.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the security team's audit concern instead of addressing what they're actually trying to protect
Arguing the design is 'better practice' in the abstract instead of showing it produces a more reliable audit trail
Reverting fully to per-user ACLs just to avoid the conflict, undermining the whole point of the group-based design
Not acknowledging the real tradeoff that review shifts to the group-design level rather than the individual level
keyPoints: Treats the security team's underlying goal (reliable audit of access) as legitimate, not the obstacle
Shows group-based access produces a more accurate, less-drifting audit trail than per-user ACLs in practice
Proposes a concrete compromise: security reviews group definitions and membership changes, not per-user-per-table grants

questions.title: Mentoring a Teammate Through a Failing Lakeflow Pipeline
questions.prompt: A junior teammate's Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline keeps failing in a way they can't diagnose, and they're about to ask you to just fix it for them. How do you use this as a mentoring moment instead of taking over, while still making sure the production issue gets resolved on a reasonable timeline?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by actually assessing urgency before deciding how hands-off to be -- if this pipeline is actively blocking something time-sensitive right now, the calculus is different than if it's failing in a way that can tolerate a few more hours of structured debugging, and the candidate should say so explicitly rather than applying one approach regardless of stakes. Assuming it's not an acute emergency, the candidate should resist the pull to just take the keyboard and fix it, since that resolves today's instance but teaches the teammate nothing they can apply next time a pipeline fails differently.

Instead, the candidate should sit with them and walk the diagnosis together: start at the pipeline's event log and expectation metrics rather than guessing, ask the teammate what they've already checked and why, and narrow the actual failure together -- is it a hard pipeline failure versus an expectation quietly dropping rows, is it a schema issue versus a transformation bug -- using questions that make the teammate do the reasoning ("what would you expect to see in the event log if it were X versus Y?") rather than the candidate announcing the answer. The goal is for the teammate to arrive at the fix themselves with scaffolding, not to watch the candidate arrive at it. The candidate should also set an explicit time-box out loud -- "let's work through this together for 30 minutes; if we're not converging, I'll step in more directly so this doesn't block the team longer than that" -- so the teammate's growth and the production need aren't actually in tension; the time-box protects both.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd actually check before deciding how hands-off to be is how urgent this really is -- if it's blocking something right now, that changes things, and I'd say that out loud rather than treating every failure the same way. But assuming it's not an active fire, my instinct is specifically not to just take over, because fixing it myself means they walk away having learned nothing they can use the next time something breaks differently.

What I'd actually do is sit down with them and work through the diagnosis together, starting from the pipeline's event log and expectation metrics instead of guessing. I'd ask them what they've already looked at and why, and then ask questions that make them do the reasoning -- "if it were a schema problem, what would you expect to see here versus if it were an expectation silently dropping rows?" -- rather than just telling them the answer. The point is for them to actually arrive at the fix, with me scaffolding it, not for me to arrive at it while they watch.

And I'd set a real time-box out loud -- something like "let's work this together for half an hour, and if we're not converging by then, I'll step in more directly so this doesn't sit broken all day." That way it's not actually a tradeoff between their growth and the production issue getting fixed -- the time-box is what protects both.
commonMistakes: Taking over and fixing it directly without assessing whether urgency actually requires that
Applying the same slow, teaching-oriented approach regardless of how time-sensitive the production issue is
Announcing the diagnosis instead of asking questions that let the teammate reason toward it themselves
Not setting an explicit time-box, leaving the mentoring approach open-ended if it isn't converging
keyPoints: Assesses actual urgency before deciding how hands-off the mentoring approach should be
Resists just fixing it directly, since that resolves this instance but teaches nothing transferable
Uses the pipeline's event log/expectation metrics and guiding questions so the teammate reasons toward the fix themselves
Sets an explicit time-box so mentoring and the production need aren't in unspoken tension

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Assesses urgency before choosing an approach rather than applying one blindly
Avoids simply taking over and fixing it directly
Describes a concrete, specific method for guiding the teammate's own diagnosis
Sets an explicit time-box balancing mentoring with the production timeline

questions.title: Negotiating a Databricks Workflows SLA With a Downstream Consumer Team
questions.prompt: A downstream BI team wants your nightly Databricks Workflow's gold tables ready by 6 AM every day, but your current pipeline, even without failures, finishes around 6:45 AM, and shortening it further would mean real cost or reliability tradeoffs. How do you negotiate this SLA conversation?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by understanding why 6 AM specifically matters to the BI team before accepting or rejecting it -- is it a hard business deadline (executives open a dashboard at 6:15), or an arbitrary round number nobody actually tested against real usage? The candidate should ask directly rather than assuming either answer, since the entire negotiation changes depending on what's really driving the number.

If it turns out to be a genuine hard requirement, the candidate should lay out the real tradeoffs honestly rather than just saying yes and quietly absorbing the risk: shortening the pipeline by 45 minutes might mean a larger/more expensive cluster, dropping a data-quality check that currently catches real issues, or accepting a higher failure rate from tighter timing margins, and the BI team should get to weigh in on which tradeoff they'd rather accept given that it's their deadline driving the cost. The candidate should also surface a middle option if one exists -- for example, publishing a subset of the most time-critical gold tables earlier while the rest finish on the current schedule, which might satisfy the actual business need without a wholesale pipeline redesign.

If it turns out 6 AM was more of an arbitrary ask than a tested business requirement, the candidate should say so plainly and propose keeping the current schedule, or something close to it, rather than accepting a riskier commitment to a a deadline nobody's actually using at the margin it's set. Either way, the answer should land on a specific, time-boxed commitment both teams actually agreed to -- not a vague "we'll try to go faster" that leaves the next missed deadline as another unresolved argument.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Before I agree to anything, I want to actually understand what's driving 6 AM specifically -- is someone opening a dashboard at 6:15 for a real decision, or is it just a round number that got picked without anyone checking what actually needs to happen by then? That changes the whole conversation, so I'd ask directly instead of guessing.

If it turns out to be real, I'm not just going to say yes and quietly eat the risk -- I'd lay out what shortening it by 45 minutes actually costs: maybe a bigger, pricier cluster, maybe dropping a quality check that's currently catching real problems, maybe just a higher chance of a late or failed run some nights because the margin gets tighter. And I'd want them in that decision, since it's their deadline driving the cost, not mine to just absorb. I'd also look for a middle path first -- can I get just the tables they actually need by 6 AM out the door earlier, while the rest finish on the current schedule? That might solve their real problem without me redesigning the whole pipeline.

If it turns out 6 AM wasn't really tested against anything, I'd say that plainly and push to keep something close to the current schedule rather than commit to a tighter number just because it was asked for. Either way, I want us to land on something specific and time-boxed that we both actually agreed to -- not a vague "we'll try to speed it up" that just turns into the same argument the next time we miss it.
commonMistakes: Agreeing to the tighter SLA immediately without understanding what's actually driving the requested time
Silently absorbing the reliability or cost risk of a tighter SLA instead of surfacing the real tradeoff to the requesting team
Not proposing a middle option, like partial early delivery of the most time-critical tables
Ending the conversation with a vague commitment to 'go faster' instead of a specific agreed-upon schedule

Surfaces the real cost/reliability tradeoffs honestly rather than silently absorbing them
Lets the requesting team weigh in on which tradeoff they'd accept, since it's their deadline driving the cost
Looks for a middle-ground option, like earlier delivery of a subset of tables
Lands on a specific, time-boxed commitment rather than a vague promise

Surfaces concrete tradeoffs honestly rather than silently absorbing risk

questions.title: Owning an Incident Where an Auto Loader Schema-Evolution Setting Silently Dropped Columns
questions.prompt: You discover that a schemaEvolutionMode setting you configured on a production Auto Loader stream three months ago has been silently dropping a column that a different team's model now depends on, and nobody noticed until their model's accuracy degraded. How do you handle owning this incident, from the first conversation with that team through the post-incident writeup?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer leads with direct ownership rather than hedged language -- the candidate configured the setting, it caused real downstream harm, and the first conversation with the affected team should say that plainly ("I set schemaEvolutionMode to none on this stream three months ago; that's why the column's been missing, and that's on me") rather than framing it as a vague shared mystery to be jointly investigated, even though some investigation legitimately still needs to happen to confirm full scope and timeline.

Before or alongside that first conversation, the candidate should move quickly to stop the ongoing damage: confirm whether a rescued-data column captured the missing field (meaning a backfill is possible) or whether it's genuinely unrecoverable from that point forward, and give the affected team a realistic timeline for getting the column flowing correctly again, rather than a vague "working on it." The candidate should also proactively surface the actual scope -- how far back the gap goes, whether other columns or other teams are plausibly affected by the same root cause -- rather than waiting to be asked, since discovering a second instance of the same problem later, after claiming it was isolated, is much worse than disclosing the full scope upfront.

The post-incident writeup should name the specific decision and its consequence without softening language, and should focus the "what changes" section on systemic fixes rather than just personal vigilance -- for example, proposing that schemaEvolutionMode default to something safer organization-wide, or that new/changed source fields trigger an automated alert rather than relying on someone eventually noticing a downstream model degrade. A writeup that concludes "I'll be more careful" without a structural change is a weak outcome for an incident whose root cause was a configuration choice, not a one-off mistake.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd lead with a direct admission in that first conversation, not a hedge -- "I configured this stream's schema evolution setting three months ago, that's why your column's been missing, and that's on me." There's still real investigation to do to nail down exact scope and timeline, but the ownership part shouldn't wait for that investigation to finish.

Before or right alongside that conversation, I want to actually stop the bleeding -- check whether there's a rescued-data column that caught the missing field, which would mean I can probably backfill it, or whether it's genuinely gone from that point forward, and give them something real instead of "I'm looking into it" -- an actual timeline for when the column's flowing correctly again. I'd also go looking for whether this is bigger than just this one column before anyone has to ask me that -- same root cause, other fields, other teams -- because finding out about a second instance later, after I said it was contained, is a much worse conversation than just disclosing the full scope now.

For the writeup, I'd name exactly what happened without softening it, and I'd spend more of it on what actually changes structurally than on "I'll be more careful going forward" -- that's not a real fix for a problem that was a configuration default, not a one-off slip. Something like proposing a safer default for that setting across the team, or an automated alert when a stream's observed fields diverge from what's actually making it into the target table, so the next version of this gets caught by a system instead of by someone noticing a model's accuracy quietly degrading months later.
commonMistakes: Softening or hedging ownership of the decision instead of stating it plainly in the first conversation
Waiting for a full investigation to complete before saying anything to the affected team
Not proactively checking and disclosing whether the issue extends beyond the one reported column or team
Writing a post-incident fix that amounts to 'be more careful' instead of a structural/systemic change
keyPoints: Leads with direct, plain ownership of the decision rather than hedged or shared-mystery framing
Moves quickly to assess recoverability (rescued-data column) and gives a real timeline, not a vague one
Proactively investigates and discloses the full scope rather than waiting to be asked
Post-incident writeup proposes a systemic fix, not just personal vigilance going forward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with direct, unhedged ownership in the first conversation
Moves quickly to assess recoverability and stop ongoing damage
Proactively investigates and discloses full scope rather than waiting to be asked
Post-incident writeup proposes a systemic fix rather than just personal vigilance

questions.title: Convincing a Team to Adopt Lakeflow Over Hand-Rolled Notebook Orchestration
questions.prompt: Your team currently runs its pipelines as a chain of manually scheduled notebooks with ad-hoc error handling, and it works, mostly. You want to migrate to Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines for the data-quality and lineage benefits, but a senior engineer who built the current system says 'if it ain't broke, don't fix it.' How do you make this case?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer takes "it ain't broke" seriously rather than dismissing it, because the senior engineer is making a real claim -- the current system has been running, presumably without catastrophic failure, and the candidate should acknowledge that rather than implying the current system is obviously bad. The actual case for Lakeflow isn't "the current thing is broken," it's "the current thing is quietly accumulating risk that 'it hasn't broken yet' doesn't rule out" -- specifically, ad-hoc error handling means failures are discovered by someone noticing bad downstream data rather than by the system itself flagging a violated expectation, and the absence of real lineage means impact analysis for any upstream change is manual and easy to get wrong.

The candidate should avoid proposing a wholesale rewrite of the working system, which is exactly the kind of disruption that validates the senior engineer's caution, and instead propose piloting Lakeflow on a new pipeline or a genuinely low-stakes existing one, letting the comparison be concrete and observed rather than argued abstractly. The candidate should also directly invite the senior engineer into evaluating that pilot -- since they built and understand the current system's real failure modes better than anyone, their judgment about whether Lakeflow's expectations/lineage actually catch something the current system would have missed is exactly the evidence that would make the case, or legitimately not make it, rather than the candidate deciding unilaterally that the pilot succeeded.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd take "it ain't broke" seriously rather than brush past it -- the system has been running, and pretending it's obviously bad isn't going to land with someone who built it and has watched it work. The case I'd actually make isn't that the current system is broken, it's that "hasn't broken yet" and "isn't quietly accumulating risk" aren't the same thing. Ad-hoc error handling means we usually find out something's wrong when someone notices bad numbers downstream, not because the pipeline itself flagged a violated expectation. And without real lineage, figuring out what breaks if we change an upstream table is a manual exercise someone has to get right every time, which is exactly the kind of thing that eventually does break, just not yet.

I wouldn't propose rewriting the whole thing -- that's the kind of disruption that proves his point. I'd rather pick a new pipeline, or some low-stakes existing one, and build it in Lakeflow as a real pilot, so the comparison is something we can both look at instead of argue about abstractly. And I'd specifically want him evaluating that pilot with me, because he understands the current system's actual failure modes better than I do -- if Lakeflow's expectations and lineage genuinely catch something our current approach would've missed, that's evidence from someone who'd actually know, not just my opinion that it's better.
commonMistakes: Dismissing 'it ain't broke' instead of acknowledging the current system's real track record
Framing the case as 'the current system is bad' instead of 'risk is accumulating quietly'
Proposing a full rewrite of the working system instead of a contained, low-stakes pilot
Deciding the pilot succeeded unilaterally instead of involving the skeptical engineer in evaluating it
keyPoints: Acknowledges the current system's real track record instead of implying it's obviously broken
Reframes the case around quietly accumulating risk, not visible brokenness
Proposes a contained pilot on a new or low-stakes pipeline rather than a wholesale rewrite
Involves the skeptical senior engineer directly in evaluating the pilot's results

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Takes the senior engineer's objection seriously rather than dismissing it
Makes a concrete case based on accumulating risk rather than claiming the current system is broken
Proposes a contained pilot instead of a wholesale rewrite
Involves the skeptical engineer directly in evaluating the pilot

questions.title: Pushing Back on an Unrealistic Timeline for a Hive Metastore to Unity Catalog Migration
questions.prompt: Your manager wants your team's entire legacy Hive metastore migrated to Unity Catalog in two weeks, driven by an executive deadline you weren't part of setting. You know from scoping it that a safe migration -- including access-control remapping and validating no broken lineage -- realistically takes six weeks. How do you push back?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer avoids both extremes: flatly refusing the two-week deadline without offering anything constructive, and quietly agreeing to it while privately doubting it's achievable. Instead, the candidate should bring the actual scoping work as the basis for the conversation -- not "I don't think two weeks is enough" as an opinion, but a breakdown of what six weeks is actually made of (access-control remapping across however many tables, lineage validation, some buffer for issues found along the way) so the manager is negotiating against real information, not a vague feeling of resistance.

The candidate should then offer a genuine tradeoff rather than just restating the six-week estimate as non-negotiable: what could actually be delivered in two weeks that gives the executive something real -- for example, migrating the highest-priority or most-visible subset of tables first, with access control carefully remapped on exactly that subset, while explicitly deferring full validation and the lower-priority tables to the following weeks. That gives the manager something concrete to take back to the executive conversation rather than either a flat "no" or a deadline quietly agreed to and likely missed or rushed unsafely.

The candidate should be explicit about what they're not willing to compromise on even under schedule pressure -- specifically, skipping access-control validation to hit two weeks, since a rushed migration that gets permissions wrong is a security incident waiting to surface, not a shortcut that saved time. Naming that line clearly, rather than letting "faster" quietly erode into "less safe" without anyone deciding that on purpose, is what separates a good answer from one that just capitulates under pressure.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't just say "two weeks isn't enough" and leave it there, and I also wouldn't quietly nod and agree to something I already know is six weeks of real work. I'd bring the actual scoping with me -- here's what's in the six weeks: access-control remapping across this many tables, lineage validation, some buffer because migrations like this always turn up something unexpected. That turns it from "I'm pushing back" into "here's what the work actually is," which is a very different conversation with a manager who's got their own pressure from above.

Then I'd come with an actual option, not just a restated deadline. What can genuinely ship in two weeks that gives the exec something real? Probably: migrate the highest-visibility tables first, do the access-control remapping properly on exactly that subset, and be explicit that full validation and the rest of the tables come in the following weeks. That gives my manager something concrete to bring back instead of a flat no or a deadline we both know is shaky.

The one thing I wouldn't bend on, even under real pressure, is skipping access-control validation to hit two weeks. A rushed migration that gets permissions wrong isn't a shortcut, it's a security incident that just hasn't surfaced yet. I'd say that part plainly rather than letting "faster" quietly turn into "less careful" without anyone actually deciding that on purpose.
commonMistakes: Flatly refusing the deadline without offering a constructive alternative
Quietly agreeing to two weeks while privately believing it's not achievable
Pushing back with a vague objection instead of a concrete breakdown of the actual scoped work
Not drawing an explicit line around what can't be compromised (access-control validation) even under schedule pressure
keyPoints: Brings a concrete scoping breakdown rather than a vague objection to the timeline
Offers a genuine phased tradeoff (highest-priority subset first) instead of a flat refusal or silent agreement
Gives the manager something concrete to take back to the executive conversation
Explicitly names what can't be compromised (access-control validation) regardless of schedule pressure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids both flat refusal and silent agreement to an unrealistic deadline
Brings concrete scoping detail rather than a vague objection
Proposes a genuine phased alternative the manager can act on
Explicitly names a non-negotiable safety boundary

questions.title: Disagreeing With a Peer Over Cluster Sizing and Cost Tradeoffs
questions.prompt: A peer engineer wants to significantly oversize the cluster for a large batch job 'just to be safe' after a recent failure, while you believe the failure was caused by a bad join strategy, not insufficient cluster size, and oversizing will just burn budget without fixing the real problem. How do you handle this disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer avoids simply asserting "you're wrong, I'm right" and instead treats the disagreement as a hypothesis gap that can actually be checked, since both the candidate and the peer are reasoning from the same failure but drawing different root causes from it. The candidate should propose actually looking at the failed job's Spark UI/query plan together -- specifically, checking for the signatures of a bad join strategy (a massive shuffle, skewed partition sizes, a sort-merge join where a broadcast would've fit) versus genuine resource exhaustion (executors actually running out of memory, spilling to disk under correctly-sized partitions) -- rather than each person continuing to argue from intuition about what probably happened.

If the evidence does point to a join strategy problem, the candidate should present that clearly but without making the peer feel wrong for proposing a safety-first instinct that's reasonable on its face -- "oversize when unsure" is a defensible default, just not the right fix for this specific root cause. The candidate should propose fixing the actual join strategy and testing it on the current cluster size first, framing oversizing as a fallback if the fix doesn't resolve it, rather than the first move -- that gives the peer a path to being reassured without the team paying for a resource increase that masks the real bug and risks the same failure resurfacing on a different, equally oversized job later. The candidate should stay collaborative throughout rather than turning this into a stance to win, since the actual shared goal -- the job succeeding reliably without wasted spend -- is the same for both of them.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't just tell him he's wrong -- I think the more useful move is to say "we're both reasoning from the same failure, let's actually look at what happened instead of guessing from intuition." I'd pull up the Spark UI or the query plan from the failed run together and check for what a bad join strategy actually looks like -- a huge shuffle, skewed partition sizes, a sort-merge join where a broadcast would've been fine -- versus what real resource exhaustion looks like, which is executors genuinely running out of memory or spilling to disk even with reasonably sized partitions. That turns it from a disagreement into something we can both just look at.

If it does turn out to be the join strategy, I'd want to present that in a way that doesn't make him feel like his instinct was dumb -- "oversize when something fails and you're not sure why" is a completely reasonable default, it's just not the fix for this particular cause. What I'd propose is: let's fix the join strategy and test it on the current cluster size first, and if that somehow doesn't resolve it, then we talk about sizing as the next move. That gives him a real path to being reassured the job will succeed, without us paying for more compute that just masks the actual bug and lets the same problem show up again on some other oversized job down the road. I'd try to keep this feeling like we're solving the same problem together, not like I'm trying to win an argument.
commonMistakes: Asserting the diagnosis is correct based on intuition instead of proposing to check the actual evidence together
Making the peer feel wrong for a reasonable safety-first instinct instead of acknowledging it's defensible, just not the fix here
Treating the disagreement as something to win rather than a shared goal of a reliable job without wasted spend
Not proposing a concrete sequence (fix and test first, size up only if needed) that gives the peer a path to being reassured
keyPoints: Proposes checking actual evidence (Spark UI/query plan) together instead of arguing from competing intuitions
Distinguishes concrete signatures of a bad join strategy from genuine resource exhaustion
Acknowledges the peer's safety-first instinct as reasonable even while disagreeing with it as the fix
Proposes fixing and testing the real cause first, with oversizing as a fallback, not the first move

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes checking concrete evidence together rather than arguing from intuition alone
Correctly distinguishes join-strategy symptoms from genuine resource exhaustion
Acknowledges the peer's instinct as reasonable while still pushing for the correct fix
Proposes a collaborative sequence rather than treating the disagreement as something to win
